disease.name: Hepatitis (A, B, and C)
disease.scientific_name: Hepatitis A — Hepatitis A Virus (HAV) Infection; Hepatitis B — Hepatitis B Virus (HBV) Infection; Hepatitis C — Hepatitis C Virus (HCV) Infection
disease.icd_10_code: B15.9 (Hepatitis A without hepatic coma); B15.0 (Hepatitis A with hepatic coma); B16.9 (Acute Hepatitis B without delta-agent); B18.1 (Chronic Hepatitis B without delta-agent); B18.2 (Chronic Hepatitis C); B17.1 (Acute Hepatitis C); K72.0 (Acute and subacute hepatic failure — fulminant hepatitis); K74.6 (Cirrhosis of liver — unspecified); C22.0 (Hepatocellular carcinoma); B19 (Unspecified viral hepatitis)
disease.category: Infectious Disease / Hepatology / Gastroenterology / Public Health

overview.description: Viral hepatitis is inflammation of the liver caused by any of five major hepatotropic viruses — Hepatitis A (HAV), Hepatitis B (HBV), Hepatitis C (HCV), Hepatitis D (HDV), and Hepatitis E (HEV). This dataset focuses on the three most clinically important and globally prevalent types: Hepatitis A, B, and C. Despite sharing the common feature of hepatic inflammation and a similar early clinical presentation (jaundice, fatigue, nausea, dark urine), these three viruses differ profoundly in their mode of transmission, natural history, treatment, and preventability. Hepatitis A is a self-limiting acute illness transmitted through contaminated food and water — completely vaccine-preventable. Hepatitis B is transmitted through blood, sexual contact, and vertically from mother to child — largely vaccine-preventable but may cause chronic disease leading to cirrhosis and liver cancer. Hepatitis C is transmitted primarily through blood — no vaccine exists, but it is now CURABLE in over 95% of cases with short-course oral direct-acting antiviral (DAA) therapy — one of the most remarkable therapeutic advances in modern medicine. Together, chronic hepatitis B and C infect approximately 354 million people globally, cause 1.1 million deaths annually, and are the leading cause of cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma (liver cancer) worldwide.
overview.affected_organ: Primarily the liver (hepatocytes — hepatic parenchymal cells); systemically: bile ducts, immune system, kidneys (glomerulonephritis), joints, skin (extrahepatic manifestations — particularly in HBV and HCV)
overview.prevalence: Hepatitis A: 1.4 million symptomatic cases annually (WHO); majority in low-to-middle income countries. Hepatitis B: 296 million people living with chronic HBV globally; 3.5-4% prevalence in India (approximately 40 million people); 820,000 deaths per year from HBV-related cirrhosis and HCC. Hepatitis C: 58 million people with chronic HCV globally; approximately 6-12 million in India; 290,000 deaths per year. Combined HBV+HCV: second only to tobacco as the leading preventable cause of cancer mortality globally.
overview.age_group: HAV: all ages; children often asymptomatic; adults have more severe illness; HBV: vertical transmission (birth) most common in endemic regions; sexual transmission in young adults; HCV: any age; IV drug use (young adults); transfusion-acquired (older adults in pre-screening era)
overview.is_contagious_note: HAV and HEV: person-to-person via fecal-oral route; HBV: blood, sexual fluids, vertical transmission; HCV: blood-to-blood transmission primarily
overview.is_curable_note: HAV: self-limiting — complete recovery in almost all cases. HBV: not curable (functional cure rare) — antiviral therapy suppresses virus but does not eradicate it from hepatocytes; treatment is usually lifelong. HCV: CURABLE in >95% of patients with 8-12 weeks of oral DAA therapy — one of the most significant medical achievements of the 21st century.
overview.is_chronic_note: HAV is never chronic — acute illness only. HBV: becomes chronic in 90% of perinatally infected infants, 25-30% of children under 5, and 5-10% of adults. HCV: becomes chronic in 75-85% of those acutely infected.
overview.key_fact: Hepatitis C (HCV) is now CURABLE in over 95% of patients with an 8-12 week course of oral tablets — yet the majority of people with HCV globally remain undiagnosed and untreated. Generic DAA medicines cost as little as Rs 4,000-8,000 for a complete course in India — making HCV elimination possible. Every undiagnosed person with HCV can be cured. FIND THEM, TEST THEM, TREAT THEM.

types.name: Hepatitis A (HAV)
types.description: An acute, self-limiting viral liver infection caused by the Hepatitis A virus — a non-enveloped, positive-sense single-stranded RNA virus belonging to the Picornaviridae family (genus Hepatovirus). HAV is transmitted exclusively via the fecal-oral route — through consumption of contaminated food and water, or direct person-to-person contact in conditions of poor sanitation. HAV replicates in hepatocytes and is excreted in high concentrations in bile and faeces. It is one of the most common vaccine-preventable diseases globally and the most common cause of acute viral hepatitis in low-income countries. HAV NEVER causes chronic infection — the immune response clears the virus completely in all immunocompetent individuals, leaving lifelong immunity.
types.virology: Single-stranded positive-sense RNA virus; non-enveloped (resistant to bile and detergents); 27-32 nm diameter; survives in environment for months (water, soil, shellfish); destroyed by heat >85°C for 1 minute, chlorination at >0.5 mg/L, UV irradiation

routes: Consumption of HAV-contaminated food or water — most common globally
Raw or undercooked shellfish (oysters, clams, mussels) — filter-feeders concentrate HAV from sewage-polluted water
Raw vegetables and fruits contaminated with faecally-polluted water (strawberries, raspberries, green onions, lettuce)
Food prepared by an infected food handler with poor hand hygiene
Person-to-person contact (close household contacts of infected person)
Travel to endemic areas with poor sanitation
Men who have sex with men (MSM) — sexual transmission (anal-oral contact)
transmission.infectivity_period: Maximum 1-2 weeks before symptom onset through 1 week after jaundice onset; HAV shedding in stool begins 2 weeks before symptoms and continues for 1-3 weeks after onset

types.natural_history: Entirely self-limiting in immunocompetent individuals — complete recovery in 99% within 1-2 months; biphasic illness (< 15% of cases): initial improvement followed by relapse (cholestatic hepatitis or relapsing hepatitis); no chronic infection ever develops; fulminant hepatic failure rare but occurs in 0.5-1% of adults (higher in elderly and those with pre-existing liver disease); lifelong immunity after natural infection
types.outcomes_by_age: Children under 6 years: 70% asymptomatic or mild illness — important source of spread without obvious illness; Older children and adults: symptomatic illness; Adults >50 years: highest risk of fulminant liver failure (1-3%)
types.immunity: Natural infection: lifelong immunity (IgG anti-HAV); Vaccination: 2-dose series provides >95% protective efficacy and likely lifelong immunity after both doses

types.name: Hepatitis B (HBV)
types.description: A potentially serious viral liver infection caused by the Hepatitis B virus — a partially double-stranded circular DNA virus belonging to the Hepadnaviridae family. HBV is one of the most efficiently transmitted blood-borne pathogens — 50-100 times more infectious than HIV. HBV infects hepatocytes and uniquely integrates its genome into host hepatocyte DNA (as covalently closed circular DNA — cccDNA), establishing a viral reservoir that current antiviral drugs cannot fully eradicate. This is why HBV is currently not curable. Chronic HBV infection progresses through recognised phases and is the leading cause of cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma globally.
types.virology: Partially double-stranded circular DNA virus (relaxed circular DNA — rcDNA); 42 nm diameter Dane particle; enveloped (HBsAg — hepatitis B surface antigen forms the outer envelope); core contains HBcAg (core antigen) and HBeAg (e antigen — marker of high viral replication); key marker of viral persistence: cccDNA (covalently closed circular DNA) in hepatocyte nucleus — the template for new viral RNA and the reason HBV cannot be eradicated with current therapies

routes: Vertical (perinatal) transmission — mother to child at birth (most common globally; accounts for majority of chronic HBV in Asia and Africa); infant infected at delivery through maternal blood and secretions
Sexual transmission — unprotected sexual intercourse (most common in low-endemic high-income countries); HBV present in blood, semen, vaginal secretions
Blood and blood products — transfusion of unscreened blood (rare in countries with universal screening); occupational needlestick injury in healthcare workers
Intravenous drug use — sharing contaminated needles and injection equipment
Horizontal transmission in childhood — household contact (sharing razors, toothbrushes, nail clippers in endemic settings); transmission by biting, scratching, or skin contact with open wounds
Unsafe medical/dental procedures — reuse of needles, unsterile equipment, unscreened blood transfusion (important in India)
Tattooing and piercing with unsterilised equipment
transmission.infectivity_period: From 1-2 months before symptom onset through the entire period of HBsAg positivity (can be lifelong in chronic infection)

types.natural_history_acute: Acute HBV: spontaneous clearance occurs in 90-95% of immunocompetent adults (vs only 10% of perinatally-infected infants); fulminant acute HBV: 0.5-1% of acute cases
types.natural_history_chronic: Chronic HBV (HBsAg positive >6 months) passes through recognised phases:

chronic_phases.features: HBsAg positive; HBeAg positive; very high HBV DNA (>10^7 IU/mL); NORMAL or minimally elevated ALT; minimal liver histological inflammation; immune system tolerates virus; common in perinatally-infected Asian patients (may last 20-30 years); NOT an indication for treatment (low response to antivirals)
chronic_phases.duration: Decades in perinatally-infected patients; shorter in adult-acquired infection

chronic_phases.phase: 2. Immune Active / Immune Clearance Phase (HBeAg Positive Chronic Hepatitis)
chronic_phases.features: HBsAg positive; HBeAg positive; HIGH HBV DNA (>20,000 IU/mL); RAISED ALT (>2× ULN); active liver inflammation and progressive fibrosis; immune system actively fighting virus; risk of cirrhosis if not treated
chronic_phases.treatment: ANTIVIRAL TREATMENT INDICATED — TDF, TAF, or entecavir

chronic_phases.phase: 3. Immune Control Phase (Inactive Carrier State / Low Replication)
chronic_phases.features: HBsAg positive; HBeAg NEGATIVE; anti-HBe POSITIVE (seroconversion from HBeAg to anti-HBe); LOW HBV DNA (<2,000 IU/mL); NORMAL ALT; minimal liver inflammation; low risk of progression; periodic monitoring required
chronic_phases.note: Not all HBeAg-negative patients are in inactive carrier state — some have HBeAg-negative chronic hepatitis B (pre-core mutants producing no HBeAg despite active replication)

chronic_phases.features: HBsAg positive; HBeAg NEGATIVE; anti-HBe positive; ELEVATED HBV DNA (>2,000 IU/mL — fluctuating); RAISED ALT (fluctuating); active inflammation; pre-core or core promoter mutations prevent HBeAg production despite active replication; most common phase in Mediterranean and South Asian patients; TREATMENT INDICATED

HBsAg NEGATIVE; anti-HBs positive; HBV DNA undetectable; occurs spontaneously in <1% per year; represents the closest to 'cure' achievable with current therapy; cccDNA may persist in hepatocytes; HBV reactivation can occur with immunosuppression even after HBsAg loss
chronic_phases.note: Goal of novel HBV cure therapies currently in clinical trials

types.risk_of_chronicity_by_age: Perinatal infection (<1 year): 90% chronic; Infection at 1-5 years: 25-50% chronic; Infection >5 years (adult): 5-10% chronic; Immunocompromised adult: 30-50% chronic
types.cirrhosis_hcc_risk: Without treatment: 15-40% of chronic HBV patients develop cirrhosis within 25 years; 5-year cumulative risk of HCC in HBV cirrhosis: 17%; HBV-related HCC can occur even WITHOUT cirrhosis (unique among hepatitis viruses); HBV DNA integration into oncogenes is directly carcinogenic

types.name: Hepatitis C (HCV)
types.description: A blood-borne viral infection of the liver caused by the Hepatitis C virus — an enveloped, positive-sense single-stranded RNA virus of the Flaviviridae family (genus Hepacivirus). HCV is characterised by its propensity to cause persistent chronic infection (75-85% of those infected) and by the extraordinary genetic diversity of its six major genotypes (GT1-6) and multiple subtypes (GT1a, 1b, 2a, 3a, etc.). Unlike HBV, HCV does not integrate into host DNA — it exists as replicating RNA in the cytoplasm of hepatocytes. This makes HCV curable with antiviral therapy. The development of direct-acting antiviral (DAA) drugs targeting HCV non-structural proteins (NS3/4A protease, NS5A, NS5B polymerase) has transformed HCV treatment from a gruelling 48-week pegylated interferon + ribavirin regimen with 50% cure rates and severe side effects, to an 8-12 week course of well-tolerated oral tablets achieving sustained virological response (SVR — considered cure) in over 95% of patients across all genotypes.
types.virology: Positive-sense single-stranded RNA virus; 55-65 nm; highly error-prone RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (NS5B) — produces ~1 trillion viral particles per day with high mutation rate; 6 major genotypes (GT1-GT6) and over 80 subtypes; GT3 predominates in India and South Asia; GT1 predominates in Europe and North America; genotype determines baseline SVR rates with older regimens but is less relevant with pangenotypic DAAs

routes: Intravenous (IV) drug use — sharing needles, syringes, and drug paraphernalia — most common transmission route in high-income countries; accounts for majority of new HCV infections

Unsafe medical and dental procedures — reuse of unsterilised needles, syringes, and surgical equipment; unscreened blood transfusion — the most important route in India historically (transfusion-related HCV now rare with universal blood screening but iatrogenic transmission from unsafe injections remains significant)
Blood transfusion and blood products before universal screening — responsible for large prevalence cohort in those transfused before 1992 (when screening was introduced)
Tattooing and body piercing with non-sterile equipment
Occupational needlestick injury — healthcare workers; risk ~3% per needlestick from HCV-positive source
Vertical (mother to child) transmission — 5-10% risk during delivery; lower than HBV; no HBIG equivalent available; no preventive intervention available

Sexual transmission — much less efficient than HBV; increased risk in: HIV-coinfected patients, MSM (particularly with traumatic sexual practices), multiple partners; monogamous heterosexual couples have very low transmission risk (<1% per year)
Household transmission — sharing razors, nail clippers, toothbrushes; less common than HBV
transmission.infectivity_period: From approximately 1-2 weeks after infection throughout the period of HCV RNA positivity (years to decades in chronic infection)

types.genotype_distribution_india: India: HCV Genotype 3 (GT3) is predominant (approximately 75-80% of cases) — important because GT3 is associated with more rapid progression to cirrhosis, higher HCC risk even without cirrhosis, higher rates of hepatic steatosis (fatty liver), and was historically harder to treat. GT1 and GT4 make up most remaining cases.
types.natural_history_acute: Acute HCV: often asymptomatic (80-90% of acute HCV infections have NO symptoms); of those acutely infected: 15-25% spontaneously clear the virus within 6 months (more common in: symptomatic acute infection, women, young patients, favourable IL28B genotype); 75-85% develop chronic infection
types.natural_history_chronic: Chronic HCV leads to progressive hepatic fibrosis over 20-30 years in most patients; progression rate highly variable: ~30% develop cirrhosis within 20 years (faster in: men, alcohol use, HIV coinfection, older age at infection, obesity, hepatic steatosis); once cirrhosis established: 1-4% per year risk of hepatic decompensation (ascites, variceal bleeding, encephalopathy) and 1-4% per year risk of HCC
types.svr_and_cure: Sustained Virological Response (SVR) = undetectable HCV RNA 12 weeks after completing treatment (SVR12) — defined as CURE; once SVR achieved: liver inflammation resolves; fibrosis may regress (even early cirrhosis); HCC risk dramatically reduced (but not zero in those with established cirrhosis — continue surveillance); extrahepatic manifestations may resolve; HCV cannot come back unless re-exposed

types.name: Hepatitis D (HDV — Delta Hepatitis)
types.description: Caused by Hepatitis D virus (HDV) — a defective RNA virus that can only infect individuals who are already infected with HBV (it requires HBsAg to form its envelope). HDV occurs as: (1) Co-infection with HBV (simultaneous acute HBV + HDV — generally resolves with HBV clearance; slightly higher risk of acute liver failure); or (2) Superinfection of chronic HBV carrier with HDV (causes severe chronic hepatitis with accelerated progression to cirrhosis; very high risk of fulminant hepatitis). HDV affects approximately 5% of chronic HBV carriers globally (approximately 15-20 million people).
types.diagnosis: Anti-HDV antibodies (IgM = acute; IgG = past or chronic); HDV RNA (active replication); test all HBsAg-positive patients for HDV when severe acute hepatitis, rapid progression to cirrhosis, or HBV with unexplained elevated disease activity
types.treatment: Pegylated interferon alfa (48-72 weeks) — only approved treatment; SVR rates only 25-30%; bulevirtide (Myrcludex B) — first approved entry inhibitor; emerging combinations. HBV vaccination prevents HDV (as HDV requires HBsAg)
types.india_note: HDV prevalence in India: 6-8% of HBsAg-positive patients; screen all HBV patients with severe or rapidly progressive disease

types.name: Hepatitis E (HEV)
types.description: An acute, usually self-limiting hepatitis caused by Hepatitis E virus — transmitted primarily through contaminated water (fecal-oral route, similar to HAV). HEV is the leading cause of acute viral hepatitis in many developing countries including India and is responsible for large-scale waterborne outbreaks. While almost always self-limiting in immunocompetent individuals, HEV causes DEVASTATING outcomes in pregnancy — a case fatality rate of 20-25% in the third trimester — making it one of the most dangerous hepatitis viruses for pregnant women. Covered briefly as context; full dataset separate.
types.transmission: Contaminated drinking water (most common); rare zoonotic transmission from undercooked pork (GT3, GT4 — developed countries); blood transfusion (rare)
key_facts: Most common cause of acute hepatitis in India — sporadic and epidemic forms
Waterborne outbreaks common in monsoon season (flooding of sewage systems)
Self-limiting in most adults (similar course to HAV)
EXTREMELY DANGEROUS in pregnancy (third trimester): 20-25% case fatality rate; causes fulminant hepatic failure, DIC, preterm delivery, foetal loss
Chronic HEV: occurs in immunocompromised patients (organ transplants, HIV) — GT3 zoonotic strain
Diagnosis: HEV IgM antibody (acute); HEV RNA (active infection)
Treatment: supportive; ribavirin for chronic HEV in immunocompromised

severity_levels.name: Mild Acute Hepatitis
severity_levels.description: Symptomatic acute viral hepatitis with jaundice and elevated liver enzymes but no signs of hepatic decompensation or coagulopathy. Most acute HAV and acute HBV presentations fall here.
severity_levels.criteria: Jaundice present; ALT elevated (typically 5-50× ULN); bilirubin elevated; INR normal (<1.3) — liver's synthetic function preserved; no encephalopathy; no ascites; able to eat and drink; not severely fatigued or incapacitated
severity_levels.functional_impact: Significant impact on quality of life (fatigue, nausea, jaundice); unable to work for several weeks; but not life-threatening
severity_levels.management: Outpatient management in most cases; supportive care — rest, adequate nutrition and hydration, complete alcohol abstinence; avoid hepatotoxic medications; monitor LFTs weekly until normalising; HAV and HEV: self-limiting — no antiviral; Acute HBV: antivirals not needed unless fulminant or prolonged; referral to hepatologist for HBV and HCV for chronic monitoring
severity_levels.criteria_for_upgrade: Rising INR >1.5; confusion or altered behaviour; severe vomiting preventing hydration; bilirubin rapidly rising; signs of fluid retention

severity_levels.name: Moderate to Severe Acute Hepatitis
severity_levels.description: Significant hepatitis with impaired hepatic synthetic function or severely disabling symptoms, but not meeting full criteria for acute liver failure.
severity_levels.criteria: Marked jaundice (bilirubin >100 mcmol/L); ALT >50× ULN; INR 1.3-1.5 (early coagulopathy); significant nausea and vomiting; unable to maintain adequate oral intake; highly elevated inflammatory markers; no encephalopathy yet
severity_levels.functional_impact: Completely incapacitated; risk of dehydration; requires hospital level monitoring
severity_levels.management: Hospital admission for monitoring; IV fluids if vomiting prevents oral intake; daily LFTs, INR, bilirubin, renal function; hepatology review; acute HBV with severe course: consider tenofovir or entecavir antiviral; avoid all hepatotoxic medications including paracetamol; fetal monitoring in pregnancy
severity_levels.criteria_for_upgrade: INR >1.5 with any encephalopathy; INR >2.0 regardless of encephalopathy; AKI developing; rapidly rising bilirubin

severity_levels.name: Acute Liver Failure (Fulminant Hepatitis)
severity_levels.description: A rare but life-threatening complication — defined as severe acute liver injury with impaired synthetic function (coagulopathy — INR ≥1.5) AND hepatic encephalopathy in a patient WITHOUT pre-existing liver disease, occurring within 26 weeks of illness onset. Acute liver failure (ALF) carries a mortality of 20-40% without liver transplantation.
severity_levels.criteria: INR ≥1.5 (coagulopathy); Hepatic encephalopathy (confusion, altered consciousness — grades 1-4); Jaundice; Often: acute kidney injury, hypoglycaemia, cerebral oedema, sepsis, multi-organ failure; HAV fulminant hepatitis: more common in elderly, those with pre-existing liver disease, and those with combined HAV + HCV or HAV + HBV; HBV fulminant hepatitis: 0.5-1% of acute HBV; HDV superinfection: higher risk
encephalopathy_grades: Grade 1: Mild confusion, altered sleep pattern, slowed mentation
Grade 2: Lethargy, moderate confusion, asterixis (flapping tremor)
Grade 3: Marked confusion, incoherent speech, sleeping but rousable
severity_levels.management: ICU admission; urgent liver transplant assessment — contact liver transplant centre immediately; IV N-acetylcysteine (NAC) — given to ALL causes of ALF (not just paracetamol); correct hypoglycaemia (10-20% glucose IV); treat cerebral oedema (head elevation 30°, mannitol); IV broad-spectrum antibiotics (prophylactic); enteral nutrition; renal replacement therapy for AKI; avoid all sedatives and hepatotoxic drugs; transplant if deteriorating despite medical therapy

severity_levels.name: Chronic Hepatitis — Compensated
severity_levels.description: Chronic HBV (>6 months HBsAg positive) or chronic HCV (>6 months HCV RNA positive) without signs of advanced liver disease or hepatic decompensation. Often asymptomatic — the majority of patients with chronic viral hepatitis do not know they are infected. Compensated means the liver is still functioning adequately despite underlying inflammation and fibrosis.
severity_levels.criteria: HBsAg positive >6 months (HBV) OR HCV RNA positive >6 months (HCV); ALT may be normal or elevated; liver fibrosis F0-F3 on Fibroscan/biopsy; no jaundice, ascites, variceal bleeding, or encephalopathy; normal or near-normal synthetic function (INR, albumin, bilirubin normal)
severity_levels.functional_impact: Often completely asymptomatic; fatigue is common; may have non-specific RUQ discomfort; quality of life may be preserved until advanced fibrosis
severity_levels.management: Regular monitoring (LFTs, HBV DNA/HCV RNA, AFP, imaging); antiviral therapy for HBV (if indicated by phase, viral load, ALT, fibrosis stage); curative DAA therapy for all patients with HCV; HCC surveillance by 6-monthly liver ultrasound + AFP in all cirrhotic patients and high-risk HBV patients; hepatology follow-up

severity_levels.name: Chronic Hepatitis — Decompensated Cirrhosis
severity_levels.description: Advanced cirrhosis with loss of hepatic synthetic and metabolic reserve — manifesting as clinical complications of portal hypertension and hepatocyte failure. Decompensation markedly reduces life expectancy (5-year survival approximately 50% without transplant vs >90% for compensated cirrhosis) and significantly impairs quality of life.
decompensation_events: Ascites — fluid accumulation in the peritoneal cavity (most common decompensation event); from portal hypertension and sodium/water retention
Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (SBP) — infection of ascitic fluid without apparent cause; occurs in 10-30% of cirrhotic patients with ascites per year; life-threatening
Variceal haemorrhage — rupture of oesophageal or gastric varices from portal hypertension; major bleeding episode mortality 15-25%
Hepatic encephalopathy — neuropsychiatric dysfunction from accumulated nitrogenous compounds (ammonia) not cleared by failing liver; ranges from minimal (grade 1) to coma (grade 4)
Hepatorenal syndrome (HRS) — functional AKI in cirrhosis from severe renal vasoconstriction; Type 1 HRS median survival 2 weeks without treatment
severity_levels.management: Hepatology and gastroenterology specialist management; ascites: sodium restriction + diuretics (spironolactone + furosemide) ± therapeutic paracentesis; SBP: IV cefotaxime + IV albumin; variceal bleeding: terlipressin + IV octreotide + band ligation endoscopy + prophylactic antibiotics; encephalopathy: lactulose + rifaximin; HCC surveillance every 3-6 months (ultrasound + AFP); liver transplant assessment — the only definitive treatment for end-stage liver disease

causative_agents_summary.hav: Hepatitis A virus (HAV) — Picornaviridae; RNA virus; fecal-oral transmission; acute self-limiting illness only
causative_agents_summary.hbv: Hepatitis B virus (HBV) — Hepadnaviridae; DNA virus; blood/sexual/vertical transmission; 5-10% of adult infections become chronic; most common cause of liver cancer globally
causative_agents_summary.hcv: Hepatitis C virus (HCV) — Flaviviridae; RNA virus; predominantly blood transmission; 75-85% of infections become chronic; now curable with DAA therapy

hav_risk_factors: Travel to HAV-endemic areas (South Asia including India, Southeast Asia, Africa, Middle East, Central and South America) — India is intermediate-to-high endemic
Consumption of raw or undercooked shellfish from polluted waters
Eating food prepared by infected food handlers with poor hygiene
Drinking contaminated water, ice, or beverages in endemic areas
Close household or sexual contact with an HAV-infected person
Children in daycare and nursery settings — spread within facilities common
Men who have sex with men (MSM) — anal-oral sexual contact
Pre-existing chronic liver disease — if infected with HAV, higher risk of fulminant hepatitis
hbv_risk_factors: Birth to an HBsAg-positive mother — single most important risk globally; perinatal transmission to infant occurs in 70-90% of HBeAg-positive mothers without prophylaxis
Unprotected sexual intercourse — particularly with HBsAg-positive partners
Intravenous drug use — sharing needles and equipment
Household contact with chronically infected person — sharing razors, toothbrushes, nail clippers; child-to-child transmission in endemic settings
Receiving unscreened blood or blood products
Tattooing, piercing, or acupuncture with unsterilised equipment
Travel to HBV-endemic regions (Sub-Saharan Africa, East and Southeast Asia, India)
India prevalence: 3.5-4% overall; higher in tribal populations, certain states (Manipur, Arunachal Pradesh, Mizoram)
hcv_risk_factors: Intravenous drug use (PWID) — most common in high-income countries; sharing any injection equipment including syringes, needles, spoons, water, cotton
Receiving blood transfusion before blood donation screening was introduced (pre-1992 in India; pre-1990 in USA/UK); haemophiliacs transfused with unscreened clotting factors
Haemodialysis — repeated blood contact; historically high transmission in dialysis units
Healthcare workers — needlestick injury; risk ~3% per percutaneous HCV-positive exposure
Tattooing, piercing, barber shop practices with shared razors/blades in India — significant transmission route
Birth to HCV-positive mother — 5-10% transmission risk during delivery
Unsafe injections from reuse of needles in medical/dental settings — major problem in India
MSM with HIV coinfection — sexual transmission of HCV more efficient
Intranasal cocaine use — sharing equipment contaminates with blood
India-specific: large cohort from transfusions (older patients); barber shop blood exposure (razors); contaminated therapeutic injections in rural settings

symptoms.overview: All three forms of viral hepatitis (A, B, C) share a similar clinical presentation when symptomatic — characterised by the classic 'hepatitis syndrome': prodromal symptoms followed by jaundice. However, many cases are ASYMPTOMATIC — particularly acute HCV (80-90%) and early chronic HBV and HCV. Symptoms when present occur in two phases: pre-icteric (before jaundice) and icteric (with jaundice).

pre_icteric_phase.duration: HAV: 3-10 days before jaundice; HBV: 1-2 weeks before jaundice
pre_icteric_phase.symptoms: Flu-like prodrome — fatigue (most prominent), low-grade fever, nausea, vomiting, anorexia (severe loss of appetite — 'even the smell of food is nauseating'), right upper quadrant discomfort or dull ache (liver tenderness), headache, myalgia (muscle aches), arthralgia (joint pains), urticaria (hives — particularly in HBV serum sickness-like phase)
pre_icteric_phase.unique_hav: Sudden and dramatic anorexia — often describes food as smelling unbearable; severe nausea; cigarette smokers often lose desire to smoke (highly suggestive of hepatitis); fever more prominent in HAV
pre_icteric_phase.unique_hbv: Serum-sickness-like syndrome in 10-20% (immune complex deposition): urticaria, arthritis, angioedema — occurring before jaundice; triggered by circulating HBsAg-anti-HBs immune complexes

icteric_phase.duration: HAV: 1-4 weeks; HBV: 2-6 weeks; HCV: if symptomatic, 2-12 weeks
symptoms: Jaundice — yellowish discolouration of skin and sclera (whites of eyes); first detected in sclera (usually when bilirubin >34-51 mcmol/L); scleral icterus is the most sensitive early sign; later involves skin (most visible in natural light)

Dark urine (bilirubinuria) — classic 'tea-coloured' or 'cola-coloured' urine from conjugated bilirubin excreted in urine; often the first symptom patients notice; one of the most sensitive clinical markers of hepatitis
Pale or clay-coloured stools (acholia) — from reduced bile excretion into the intestine; stools appear pale grey/white/putty-coloured
Pruritus (itching) — from bile salt deposition in skin; can be severe in cholestatic hepatitis
Hepatomegaly — enlarged, tender liver on palpation; right upper quadrant fullness and dull aching pain
Splenomegaly — enlarged spleen from portal hypertension (more prominent in chronic disease)
Weight loss — from nausea, anorexia, and reduced calorie intake during illness
Worsening fatigue — often the most debilitating symptom

phases.recovery_phase_hav: Gradual improvement over 1-4 weeks; jaundice fades; urine normalises; appetite returns; fatigue may persist for weeks to months after jaundice resolution; complete recovery in almost all cases

primary_symptoms.name: Fatigue and Profound Malaise
primary_symptoms.description: The most universal and often the most disabling symptom across all forms of hepatitis. In acute hepatitis: sudden onset of extreme fatigue and inability to function normally — patients describe it as 'the worst fatigue of their life'. In chronic hepatitis B and C: fatigue is often the only symptom for years — a persistent, low-grade but significantly impactful tiredness that does not improve with rest and impairs work, concentration, and quality of life. Fatigue from chronic hepatitis is multifactorial: direct viral effects on the central nervous system, cytokine-mediated sickness behaviour, anaemia (if cirrhotic), and depressive effect of chronic illness.
primary_symptoms.onset: Acute hepatitis: sudden (days); Chronic: insidious (months to years)
primary_symptoms.clinical_importance: Fatigue combined with dark urine in any patient should immediately raise suspicion for hepatitis — send LFTs urgently

primary_symptoms.name: Jaundice (Icterus)
primary_symptoms.description: Yellowish discolouration of the skin, mucous membranes, and sclera (whites of the eyes) — caused by elevated serum bilirubin (>34-51 mcmol/L). Bilirubin accumulates when hepatocyte dysfunction impairs conjugation and excretion of bilirubin from haem metabolism. Scleral icterus (yellow eyes) is the most sensitive early sign — first detected when bilirubin exceeds 34 mcmol/L; jaundice in the skin is visible when bilirubin >51 mcmol/L. Jaundice is best assessed in natural daylight — fluorescent lighting can mask or distort yellow colour. Deep jaundice (bilirubin >300 mcmol/L) indicates severe disease.
primary_symptoms.onset: Acute hepatitis: appears 3-10 days after prodrome; Chronic: usually absent until advanced disease
primary_symptoms.note: The combination of yellow eyes (jaundice) + dark urine + pale stools = CLASSIC hepatitis triad — requires immediate medical attention and LFTs

primary_symptoms.name: Dark Urine (Tea/Cola-Coloured Urine)
primary_symptoms.description: Dark amber, tea-coloured, or cola-brown urine — from conjugated bilirubin excreted by the kidneys when hepatocytes are unable to process bilirubin normally. Often the first symptom that patients notice and bring to medical attention — predates visible skin or eye jaundice. The urine does not clear with increased fluid intake (distinguishing it from simply concentrated urine from dehydration). Bilirubin is easily detected on urine dipstick.
primary_symptoms.onset: Often the FIRST symptom noticed by patients — appears 1-3 days before visible jaundice

primary_symptoms.name: Nausea, Vomiting, and Severe Anorexia
primary_symptoms.description: Severe loss of appetite (anorexia) is a hallmark of acute hepatitis — often dramatic and very specific. Patients describe an inability to eat, with even the sight or smell of food causing nausea. Cigarette smokers losing their desire to smoke during an illness is historically considered highly suggestive of acute hepatitis. Vomiting is common, especially in HAV. In HCV acute infection: these symptoms are often minimal or absent (majority asymptomatic). In chronic hepatitis: nausea may occur in advanced disease from elevated ammonia in hepatic encephalopathy.

primary_symptoms.name: Right Upper Quadrant Pain and Hepatomegaly
primary_symptoms.description: Dull, aching pain or discomfort in the right upper quadrant of the abdomen (under the right rib cage) — from distension of the liver capsule (Glisson's capsule) as hepatocytes swell with inflammation. On examination: hepatomegaly (enlarged liver) is palpable in the majority of patients with acute hepatitis; the liver edge is smooth, rounded, and tender to palpation. Severe, sharp, constant right upper quadrant pain may indicate complications (pericholecystitis, abscess, hepatic vein thrombosis).
primary_symptoms.note: Acute hepatitis is a common cause of misdiagnosis as biliary colic or cholecystitis — always check LFTs and viral serology in any patient with RUQ pain

primary_symptoms.name: Fever
primary_symptoms.description: Low-grade to moderate fever is common in the pre-icteric phase of acute hepatitis, particularly HAV. HAV typically produces a more prominent fever (38-39°C) than HBV or HCV. High fever (>39°C) is unusual in uncomplicated acute hepatitis and should prompt investigation for a complication or alternative diagnosis. In chronic hepatitis: fever is absent unless there is an acute bacterial complication (SBP, cholangitis, HCC with tumour fever).
primary_symptoms.severity: Mild to Moderate in acute; absent in chronic

secondary_symptoms: Pruritus (severe itching) — particularly in cholestatic hepatitis from bile salt deposition in skin; may be generalised; worsens at night
Pale/clay/putty-coloured stools — from reduced bile reaching intestine (acholic stools); waxy grey-white appearance
Weight loss — from nausea and anorexia; significant weight loss in decompensated cirrhosis (ascites may mask true weight loss)
Arthralgia and myalgia — joint and muscle pains in pre-icteric phase; serum-sickness-like syndrome in 10-20% of acute HBV
Urticaria (hives) and skin rash — immune complex deposition in acute HBV; palpable purpura in HCV-related mixed cryoglobulinaemia
Splenomegaly — enlarged spleen from portal hypertension in chronic hepatitis with fibrosis/cirrhosis
Peripheral oedema and ascites — from hypoalbuminaemia and portal hypertension in decompensated cirrhosis
Confusion and cognitive impairment (hepatic encephalopathy) — ammonia accumulation in advanced liver disease
Spider naevi — dilated superficial blood vessels radiating from a central arteriole on upper body; sign of cirrhosis from oestrogen metabolism failure
Palmer erythema — redness of thenar and hypothenar eminences; sign of chronic liver disease
Leuconychia (white nails) and Terry's nails — white discolouration; sign of hypoalbuminaemia in cirrhosis
Gynaecomastia (breast development in men) and testicular atrophy — from impaired oestrogen metabolism in cirrhosis
Caput medusae — dilated abdominal wall veins radiating from umbilicus; sign of portal hypertension
Haematemesis or melaena — vomiting blood or black tarry stools from oesophageal variceal bleeding in portal hypertension — EMERGENCY

hbv_extrahepatic: Polyarteritis nodosa (PAN) — systemic vasculitis of medium arteries; fever, weight loss, renal disease, peripheral neuropathy, skin lesions (livedo reticularis); ~30% of PAN cases are HBV-related
Membranous nephropathy — HBV antigen-antibody complex deposition in glomeruli causing nephrotic syndrome
Mixed essential cryoglobulinaemia — similar to HCV
hcv_extrahepatic: Mixed cryoglobulinaemia — most common HCV extrahepatic manifestation (40-60% of chronic HCV patients have detectable cryoglobulins); immune complex vasculitis causing: palpable purpura (lower legs), arthralgia, peripheral neuropathy, membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis
Membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis (MPGN) — HCV immune complex deposition; proteinuria, haematuria, renal impairment
Lichen planus — white lacy patches on oral mucosa; HCV associated in 30-40% of lichen planus cases
Porphyria cutanea tarda (PCT) — blistering skin disease; HCV triggers PCT in genetically susceptible individuals
Non-Hodgkin lymphoma (B-cell) — 2-3 fold increased risk in chronic HCV; related to chronic B-lymphocyte stimulation by HCV
Sjögren's syndrome — dry eyes and dry mouth
Diabetes mellitus type 2 — HCV promotes insulin resistance; resolves with SVR in some patients
Depression and fatigue — HCV neuropsychiatric effects; independent of liver disease severity; resolves with SVR in many

warning_signs: Confusion, altered consciousness, or irrational behaviour in a hepatitis patient — possible hepatic encephalopathy — EMERGENCY
INR >1.5 in acute hepatitis — early coagulopathy; liver transplant assessment urgently needed
Haematemesis (vomiting blood) or melaena (black tarry stools) — variceal bleeding in portal hypertension — LIFE-THREATENING EMERGENCY — call 102/112
Rapid increase in abdominal girth or new abdominal distension — possible ascites from decompensation
Fever with abdominal pain in patient with known ascites — possible spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (SBP) — EMERGENCY
Hypoglycaemia (cold sweats, confusion, trembling) in severe acute hepatitis — liver failing to maintain blood glucose — hospital immediately
Rapidly deepening jaundice with deteriorating consciousness — fulminant hepatic failure
Pregnancy + jaundice + any hepatitis symptoms — always urgent assessment (HEV in pregnancy is life-threatening)

medical_history: Onset and duration of symptoms — acute (days-weeks) vs chronic (months-years, often asymptomatic); jaundice onset; colour of urine and stools
Travel history — recent travel to HAV/HEV-endemic areas (India rural, Southeast Asia, Africa); when did travel occur relative to symptoms (incubation period guides pathogen)
Dietary history — shellfish consumption (raw oysters, mussels, clams); food and water source during travel; street food
Vaccination history — HAV vaccination (2 doses); HBV vaccination (3 doses); were vaccinations complete?
Blood transfusion history — date, country, pre or post-screening era (pre-1992 in India = HCV/HBV risk)
Injection drug use history — IV, IM, or subcutaneous; needle sharing; current or past; non-judgmental questioning
Sexual history — HBsAg-positive partner; multiple partners; MSM; HIV status
Tattooing, body piercing, or traditional practices — dates; whether sterile equipment used; barber shop shaving in India
Healthcare exposure — recent surgery, dental procedures, endoscopy, injections in healthcare settings particularly in India
Occupation — healthcare worker (needlestick risk); food handler (HAV transmission source)
Family history — HBV in family members (perinatal or horizontal transmission in childhood); autoimmune liver disease
Alcohol consumption — quantity, frequency, duration; alcohol potentiates viral hepatitis-related fibrosis dramatically; alcohol alone can cause hepatitis (important differential)

Medications and supplements — paracetamol (acetaminophen) overdose or therapeutic doses in alcoholics (drug-induced liver injury — DILI); herbal and Ayurvedic medicines (several cause DILI — e.g., Kava, hepatotoxic Ayurvedic preparations); anti-TB drugs (isoniazid, pyrazinamide, rifampicin all hepatotoxic)
HIV status — HIV coinfection dramatically worsens HBV and HCV outcomes and requires integrated management
Contact with a known case — household contact with jaundiced person (HAV); HBsAg-positive sexual partner or family member (HBV)
Previous hepatitis testing — known HBsAg positive? Known HCV antibody positive? If so, were they followed up and treated?
Pregnancy status — critical: HEV in pregnancy is life-threatening; HBV requires PMTCT; HCV DAAs not licensed in pregnancy
physical_examination: Vital signs — temperature (fever in acute hepatitis); blood pressure; heart rate; weight (baseline for monitoring)

Jaundice assessment — inspect sclera (best in natural light; yellow = icterus); skin colour (yellow tinge in natural light); inspect subungual region (under fingernails); hard palate (yellow mucosa); level of jaundice correlates roughly with bilirubin level
INSPECTION: abdominal distension (ascites); caput medusae (dilated abdominal wall veins from portal hypertension); visible peristalsis (obstruction differential)

PALPATION: hepatomegaly — liver edge smooth and tender in acute hepatitis; firm and irregular in cirrhosis; assess liver span (percussion); splenomegaly — tip palpable in portal hypertension; shifting dullness and fluid thrill for ascites detection
PERCUSSION: shifting dullness (ascites — fluid moves with position change); liver dullness (span — normally 12-15 cm); Traube's space (gastric tympany — obliterated in splenomegaly)

Skin examination: spider naevi (dilated capillaries, upper body — >5 suggests chronic liver disease); palmer erythema; scratch marks from pruritus; palpable purpura (lower limbs — HCV cryoglobulinaemia); jaundice depth; bruising or petechiae (coagulopathy); xanthelasma (cholestatic liver disease)
Nail changes: leuconychia (white nails — hypoalbuminaemia); Terry's nails (white proximal, normal distal — cirrhosis); clubbing (chronic liver disease, HCC)
Signs of chronic liver disease: gynaecomastia (breast tissue in males — oestrogen excess from impaired liver metabolism); testicular atrophy; loss of body hair; parotid enlargement (alcohol-related)

Neurological examination: asterixis (flapping tremor) — outstretched hands 'flap' — pathognomonic of hepatic encephalopathy; perform finger-nose test, cognitive assessment (mini-mental state), constructional apraxia (inability to draw a 5-pointed star)
Fetor hepaticus — characteristic sweet-musty breath from mercaptans; sign of advanced liver disease
Peripheral oedema — bilateral pitting ankle oedema from hypoalbuminaemia and portal hypertension

diagnostic_tests.description: The essential initial blood tests for any suspected hepatitis. Include: ALT (alanine aminotransferase — most liver-specific; rises dramatically in acute hepatocyte injury); AST (aspartate aminotransferase — less specific but elevated; AST:ALT ratio >2:1 suggests alcoholic hepatitis); ALP (alkaline phosphatase — elevated in cholestatic disease — bile duct obstruction or intrahepatic cholestasis); GGT (gamma-glutamyltransferase — sensitive marker of liver injury especially from alcohol and certain drugs); Total and direct bilirubin; Albumin (falls in chronic liver disease — reflects synthetic function); Total protein.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Confirm hepatocyte injury; quantify severity; distinguish hepatocellular (high ALT/AST) from cholestatic (high ALP/GGT/bilirubin) pattern; monitor disease course and treatment response
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: ALT >10× ULN (Upper Limit of Normal): significant hepatitis; ALT >50× ULN (typically >1,000 U/L): severe hepatitis; ALT >200× ULN: acute liver failure risk; Bilirubin >100 mcmol/L: significant jaundice; Albumin <30 g/L: impaired synthetic function; ALP >3× ULN with high bilirubin and normal ALT: consider biliary obstruction or infiltrative disease
diagnostic_tests.acute_hepatitis_pattern: Very high ALT (often 1,000-5,000 U/L); high bilirubin; ALP relatively less elevated — HEPATOCELLULAR pattern
diagnostic_tests.monitoring: Acute hepatitis: LFTs weekly until normalising; Chronic hepatitis on treatment: 3-monthly

diagnostic_tests.description: The prothrombin time (PT) and INR (International Normalised Ratio) measure the time taken for blood to clot via the extrinsic coagulation pathway — dependent on Vitamin K-dependent clotting factors (II, VII, IX, X) synthesised exclusively by the liver. Because the liver has a massive synthetic reserve, INR only rises when >70-80% of hepatic function is lost. Therefore, elevated INR in acute hepatitis is a critical warning sign of severe hepatic failure.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Assess hepatic synthetic function; guide severity classification; identify patients needing liver transplant listing; monitor liver function in chronic liver disease
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: INR <1.3: normal; INR 1.3-1.5: mild coagulopathy — close monitoring; INR >1.5 + encephalopathy = Acute Liver Failure (ALF definition); INR >2.0 in acute hepatitis = severe disease — hepatology and liver transplant referral; INR >6.0 = extremely poor prognosis without transplant

diagnostic_tests.test_name: HAV Serology — Anti-HAV IgM and Anti-HAV IgG
diagnostic_tests.description: Hepatitis A serological testing — the standard diagnostic test for HAV infection and immunity assessment. Anti-HAV IgM: appears within 5-10 days of infection onset; peaks in first month; persists for 3-6 months — the DIAGNOSTIC MARKER of acute HAV infection. Anti-HAV IgG: appears weeks after IgM; persists lifelong — marker of past infection (immunity) or successful vaccination.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Diagnose acute HAV infection; assess HAV immunity before travel or vaccination; confirm vaccination effectiveness
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: Anti-HAV IgM POSITIVE = ACUTE HEPATITIS A (current infection); Anti-HAV IgM negative + IgG positive = Past infection or successful vaccination (immune); Both negative = Never infected, never vaccinated — susceptible (vaccinate)
diagnostic_tests.note: Anti-HAV IgM may occasionally give false-positive results — always interpret in clinical context; Acute hepatitis symptoms + positive IgM = diagnose

diagnostic_tests.test_name: HBV Serology Panel — HBsAg, Anti-HBs, Anti-HBc IgM, Anti-HBc Total, HBeAg, Anti-HBe
diagnostic_tests.description: A panel of serological markers that together provide comprehensive information on HBV infection status, phase of disease, replication activity, and immune response. Interpretation requires understanding all markers in combination.

markers.meaning: MARKER OF CURRENT HBV INFECTION — the envelope protein of HBV; positive = either acute or chronic HBV; if positive for >6 months = CHRONIC HBV
markers.clinical_use: Screening test for HBV; first test to order when HBV suspected

markers.meaning: MARKER OF IMMUNITY — protective antibody; positive = immune, either from vaccination (HBsAg negative + Anti-HBs positive) or past resolved infection (anti-HBc positive + anti-HBs positive); level >10 mIU/mL = protective immunity from vaccination
markers.clinical_use: Confirm vaccination response; assess immunity in healthcare workers

markers.marker: Anti-HBc IgM (IgM Antibody to HBV Core Antigen)
markers.meaning: MARKER OF ACUTE OR RECENT HBV INFECTION — the immune response to the core protein; high titre IgM = acute infection; low titre IgM may persist or recur during reactivation
markers.clinical_use: Distinguish acute HBV (IgM positive) from chronic HBV (IgM negative, IgG positive); essential when HBsAg positive to determine if acute or chronic

markers.marker: Anti-HBc Total (IgG + IgM) (Total Antibody to HBV Core Antigen)
markers.meaning: MARKER OF PAST OR CURRENT INFECTION — positive in acute, chronic, AND resolved infection; never positive from vaccination alone (core protein not in current vaccines); anti-HBc positive + HBsAg negative + anti-HBs positive = RESOLVED PAST INFECTION; anti-HBc positive + HBsAg negative + anti-HBs negative = PAST INFECTION (window period or low-level chronic — occult HBV)
markers.clinical_use: Determine prior exposure; screen blood donors; diagnose occult HBV; determine need for vaccination vs treatment

markers.meaning: MARKER OF HIGH VIRAL REPLICATION — the secreted form of HBcAg; positive = high-level viral replication; associated with high HBV DNA levels (>10^6 IU/mL); indicates high infectivity; typically positive in immune-tolerant and immune-active phases
markers.clinical_use: Assess replication phase; guide treatment decisions; monitor treatment response (HBeAg seroconversion = important treatment milestone)

markers.meaning: MARKER OF LOWER REPLICATION — seroconversion from HBeAg to anti-HBe indicates reduction in viral replication; anti-HBe positive + low HBV DNA = inactive carrier state; anti-HBe positive + elevated HBV DNA = HBeAg-negative chronic hepatitis (pre-core mutants)
markers.clinical_use: Assess phase of infection; monitor HBeAg seroconversion during treatment

key_interpretation_patterns: HBsAg+ / Anti-HBc IgM+ / HBeAg+ / Anti-HBs- = ACUTE HEPATITIS B
HBsAg+ / Anti-HBc IgG+ / HBeAg+ / HBV DNA HIGH = CHRONIC HEPATITIS B (HBeAg positive — immune active or tolerant)
HBsAg+ / Anti-HBc IgG+ / HBeAg- / Anti-HBe+ / HBV DNA LOW = INACTIVE CARRIER (immune control)
HBsAg+ / Anti-HBc IgG+ / HBeAg- / Anti-HBe+ / HBV DNA HIGH = HBeAg-NEGATIVE CHRONIC HEPATITIS B
HBsAg- / Anti-HBs+ / Anti-HBc- = VACCINATED (immune from vaccination — never infected)
HBsAg- / Anti-HBs+ / Anti-HBc+ = RESOLVED PAST INFECTION (immune)
HBsAg- / Anti-HBs- / Anti-HBc- = NEVER INFECTED, NEVER VACCINATED — susceptible; vaccinate

diagnostic_tests.description: Quantitative measurement of HBV DNA in serum — the direct measure of viral replication activity. HBV DNA is the most important test for determining the need for antiviral treatment, monitoring treatment response, and predicting progression risk. Reported in IU/mL (International Units) or copies/mL (1 IU ≈ 5.6 copies).
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Determine viral replication level; guide treatment initiation threshold; monitor treatment response (target: undetectable HBV DNA on therapy); detect viral resistance; predict HCC risk (HBV DNA >2,000 IU/mL associated with significantly higher HCC risk even without cirrhosis)
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: Undetectable (<20 IU/mL): inactive or on effective treatment; >2,000 IU/mL: treatment consideration threshold; >20,000 IU/mL HBeAg-negative: strong treatment indication; >200,000 IU/mL HBeAg-positive: immune-active phase; Treatment target: undetectable HBV DNA on therapy
diagnostic_tests.monitoring: At diagnosis; before treatment; 3-monthly during treatment; annually when inactive carrier

diagnostic_tests.description: Third-generation enzyme immunoassay (EIA) detecting antibodies to multiple HCV antigens (NS3, NS4, NS5 proteins, and core). Anti-HCV is the standard screening test for HCV exposure. Becomes positive 4-10 weeks after infection (antibody window period). A positive anti-HCV means the person HAS BEEN EXPOSED to HCV — but does NOT distinguish between active current infection (HCV RNA positive) and past resolved infection (HCV RNA negative). All anti-HCV-positive results MUST be confirmed with HCV RNA testing.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Screen for HCV exposure; identify individuals who need further testing (HCV RNA); public health surveillance
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: Anti-HCV POSITIVE: further testing required (HCV RNA); Anti-HCV NEGATIVE in high-risk patient or within first 6 months of potential exposure: repeat HCV RNA testing — antibodies may not yet be detectable
diagnostic_tests.important_limitation: Anti-HCV DOES NOT confirm active infection — a positive anti-HCV test means either current infection OR past resolved infection; always confirm with HCV RNA; Anti-HCV may be negative (false negative) in severely immunocompromised patients despite active infection — test HCV RNA directly in such patients

diagnostic_tests.test_name: HCV RNA (Viral Load / HCV PCR) — Confirmatory and Monitoring Test
diagnostic_tests.description: Quantitative real-time PCR measuring HCV RNA in serum — the definitive test for active HCV infection. HCV RNA is detectable 1-2 weeks after infection (before anti-HCV becomes positive). HCV RNA is positive in active infection and negative after spontaneous clearance or successful DAA treatment (SVR). Required to confirm active infection in all anti-HCV-positive patients. Treatment monitoring: HCV RNA measured at baseline, during, and 12 weeks after treatment completion (SVR12 = undetectable = CURE).
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Confirm active HCV infection (all anti-HCV-positive patients); baseline viral load before treatment; monitor treatment response; confirm SVR12 (cure); diagnose HCV in window period before anti-HCV detectable; diagnose HCV in immunocompromised where anti-HCV may be falsely negative
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: Detectable HCV RNA: ACTIVE INFECTION — requires treatment; Undetectable HCV RNA: either early acute infection (before antibodies) OR cleared infection (past or after treatment); SVR12 = HCV RNA undetectable 12 weeks after completing DAA treatment = CURE

diagnostic_tests.description: Determines the HCV genotype (GT1-GT6) and subtype (GT1a, GT1b, GT3a, etc.) from serum HCV RNA. HCV genotype was critically important for selecting treatment with older interferon-based regimens. With modern pangenotypic DAAs (sofosbuvir/velpatasvir; glecaprevir/pibrentasvir), genotype is less critical — these regimens cure all genotypes. However, genotype remains important for: selecting optimal treatment duration (GT3 may require 12 weeks); predicting response in certain patient subgroups; determining need for ribavirin addition.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Guide treatment regimen and duration selection; predict natural history (GT3 associated with faster fibrosis, higher HCC risk); epidemiological surveillance
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: GT1 (1a, 1b): most common globally; GT3: most common in India (75-80%), Pakistan, South Asia; GT4: Middle East, Africa; GT2: less common; GT5/6: rare
diagnostic_tests.india_note: In India, GT3 predominates (75-80% of HCV); GT3 is the most challenging genotype — associated with hepatic steatosis (fatty liver), faster fibrosis progression, and higher risk of HCC even in non-cirrhotic patients

diagnostic_tests.test_name: Liver Fibrosis Assessment — FibroScan (Transient Elastography) and APRI/FIB-4 Scores
diagnostic_tests.description: Determining the degree of liver fibrosis is critical for deciding treatment urgency and predicting outcomes in chronic HBV and HCV. FibroScan (transient elastography — TE) measures liver stiffness in kilopascals (kPa) — stiffer liver = more fibrosis. Non-invasive, painless, immediate result, outpatient procedure. APRI (AST to Platelet Ratio Index) and FIB-4 (age × AST / platelets × ALT) are simple blood-test-based scores that estimate fibrosis — useful when FibroScan is not available (India rural settings).
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Stage liver fibrosis without biopsy (non-invasive); identify cirrhosis (F4) requiring HCC surveillance; guide treatment urgency; monitor fibrosis regression after successful treatment
diagnostic_tests.fibroscan_values: Liver stiffness <6 kPa: F0-F1 (minimal fibrosis); 6-8 kPa: F2 (moderate); 8-11 kPa: F3 (significant fibrosis); >11-13 kPa: F4 (cirrhosis); >20 kPa: severe cirrhosis; >25 kPa: portal hypertension likely
diagnostic_tests.apri_score: APRI >0.5 suggests significant fibrosis (F≥2); APRI >1.0 suggests cirrhosis (F4) — widely used in resource-limited settings
diagnostic_tests.liver_biopsy: Gold standard but invasive — now rarely needed with good non-invasive methods; reserved for: discordant non-invasive test results; suspected additional liver disease (e.g., NAFLD + HCV); atypical presentations
diagnostic_tests.monitoring: FibroScan baseline before treatment; after SVR: every 1-2 years; annually in cirrhosis

diagnostic_tests.test_name: Alpha-Fetoprotein (AFP) and Liver Ultrasound — HCC Surveillance
diagnostic_tests.description: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) surveillance is mandatory in all patients with cirrhosis from chronic HBV or HCV, and in certain HBV patients even without cirrhosis. AFP is a tumour marker elevated in 60-70% of HCC cases but has low sensitivity and specificity alone. Liver ultrasound detects focal liver lesions. The combination of 6-monthly ultrasound + AFP provides the recommended HCC surveillance programme — any lesion detected requires further characterisation by multiphasic CT or MRI.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Early detection of HCC (when curative treatment — resection or ablation — is still possible); monitor for HCC development in high-risk groups
hcc_surveillance_indications: All patients with HBV-related or HCV-related cirrhosis (F4 on FibroScan)
HBV patients with family history of HCC
HBV patients with high HBV DNA despite therapy
Asian HBV patients: men over 40 years, women over 50 years (even without cirrhosis)
HCV patients with GT3 (higher HCC risk even pre-cirrhosis)
diagnostic_tests.frequency: Liver ultrasound + AFP every 6 months; multiphasic CT or MRI for suspicious lesions >1 cm
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: AFP >20 ng/mL: investigate; AFP >200 ng/mL with typical vascular liver lesion on imaging: highly suspicious for HCC; AFP >400 ng/mL: very high specificity for HCC

diagnostic_tests.test_name: Complete Blood Count (FBC), Renal Function, and Metabolic Panel
diagnostic_tests.description: Essential baseline and monitoring tests. FBC in cirrhosis: thrombocytopaenia (low platelets) from splenic sequestration in portal hypertension — the first sign of developing cirrhosis; anaemia (normochromic normocytic from chronic disease or macrocytic from alcohol or folate deficiency); leucopaenia (hypersplenism). Renal function: critical before and during DAA treatment; HCV-related cryoglobulinaemia causes renal impairment; cirrhotics at risk of hepatorenal syndrome.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Assess baseline health status; detect portal hypertension markers (thrombocytopaenia, splenomegaly); guide antiviral dosing (renal function); monitor for drug toxicity
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: Platelets <150,000: investigate for cirrhosis; Platelets <100,000: likely significant portal hypertension; eGFR <30: adjust DAA dosing (sofosbuvir requires dose adjustment below eGFR 30)

diagnostic_tests.description: Co-infection testing is essential in all patients with HBV or HCV: HIV coinfection dramatically worsens outcomes of both HBV (faster fibrosis, higher HCC risk) and HCV (faster cirrhosis, reduced spontaneous clearance). HDV must be screened in all HBsAg-positive patients — HDV superinfection causes accelerated liver disease. HEV IgM should be tested in all acute hepatitis where HAV and HBV serology is negative.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Detect clinically critical coinfections; guide integrated treatment approach; prevent missed diagnoses
diagnostic_tests.testing: HIV Ag/Ab combo test (4th generation — detects antigen and antibodies); Anti-HDV IgM + HDV RNA in all HBsAg-positive; HEV IgM in unexplained acute hepatitis

diagnostic_tests.test_name: Thyroid Function Tests (TFTs) — Pre-Treatment for Interferon
diagnostic_tests.description: Pegylated interferon (PegIFN) — used for chronic HBV — commonly causes thyroid dysfunction (autoimmune thyroiditis, hypothyroidism or hyperthyroidism) in 4-20% of patients. Baseline TFTs (TSH, Free T4) must be measured before starting PegIFN and every 3 months during treatment. Less relevant for DAA therapy (HCV) and nucleos(t)ide analogues (HBV) which have minimal thyroid effects.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Baseline thyroid function before interferon therapy; monitor for interferon-induced thyroiditis during treatment
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: TSH outside normal range before IFN: review suitability carefully; TSH abnormal during IFN: manage thyroid disorder; do not automatically stop IFN — can manage concurrently if mild

medicines.note: Hepatitis A and uncomplicated Hepatitis E have no specific antiviral treatment — supportive care only. Hepatitis B requires long-term antiviral therapy in eligible patients — treatment suppresses but does not cure HBV. Hepatitis C is now CURABLE in >95% of cases with 8-12 weeks of oral direct-acting antiviral (DAA) therapy — no injections, minimal side effects, and widely available as affordable generic medications in India. All treatment decisions require specialist hepatology or gastroenterology input.
treatment_principles: 1. HAV and uncomplicated acute HEV: NO antivirals — supportive treatment only; complete rest, adequate nutrition, hydration, strict alcohol abstinence, no hepatotoxic medications
2. Acute HBV: antivirals not routinely needed (95% of adults spontaneously clear); consider tenofovir if: prolonged severe acute HBV, INR rising, or fulminant hepatitis

3. Chronic HBV: first-line treatment is TDF (tenofovir disoproxil fumarate) or TAF (tenofovir alafenamide) — preferred for their high barrier to resistance; entecavir is alternative; lifelong treatment in most patients; treatment goal: undetectable HBV DNA, normalise ALT, prevent cirrhosis and HCC

4. Chronic HCV: treat ALL patients with detectable HCV RNA regardless of fibrosis stage, ALT level, or symptoms — the WHO and AASLD strongly endorse test-and-treat; pangenotypic DAAs are preferred; SVR = CURE; generic formulations in India make this affordable
5. ABSOLUTE contraindications to treatment: untreated decompensated liver disease for certain DAAs; pregnancy for ribavirin; pre-existing depression or serious psychiatric illness for interferon
6. All patients with chronic HBV or HCV must have complete alcohol abstinence — alcohol accelerates fibrosis synergistically with viral hepatitis
7. HBV PMTCT (Prevention of Mother to Child Transmission): TDF from week 24-28 of pregnancy in HBeAg-positive mothers; HBIG + HBV vaccine at birth to neonate regardless of maternal status
8. Maintain full HBV vaccination (3 doses) in all unvaccinated household contacts of HBsAg-positive patients

categories.purpose: Manage symptoms, prevent complications, and support hepatic recovery in acute hepatitis A, B, and E.

medicines.name: Oral Rehydration and IV Fluids
medicines.form: Oral fluids; IV Ringer's Lactate or Normal Saline
medicines.dosage: Adequate oral fluids (minimum 2.5-3L daily); IV if vomiting prevents oral intake
medicines.use_case: Prevent dehydration from nausea and vomiting in acute hepatitis; maintain adequate urine output; electrolyte replacement if vomiting is severe
medicines.note: ORS sachets (WHO formulation) are highly effective for mild-moderate dehydration from vomiting in acute hepatitis; IV dextrose-containing fluids (5-10% dextrose) may be needed for hypoglycaemia in severe acute hepatitis

medicines.name: Paracetamol (Acetaminophen) — Use With Caution
medicines.dosage: 500 mg every 6-8 hours (MAXIMUM 2g per day in acute hepatitis — NOT the standard 4g daily maximum); reduce to 1g/day maximum in significant hepatitis; use for shortest duration needed
medicines.use_case: Fever and discomfort in acute hepatitis; NOT first-line — prefer alternatives; SAFE at LOW doses even in hepatitis (widely feared but evidence shows safe at doses ≤2g/day in non-alcoholic hepatitis); paracetamol can be used cautiously in acute HAV at reduced doses for fever/discomfort
medicines.warning: Paracetamol is the MOST COMMON cause of acute liver failure in Western countries at overdose or therapeutic doses in alcoholics; in ACTIVE HEPATITIS — maximum 2g/day; in alcohol-related hepatitis or alcoholics — AVOID completely; NSAIDs also contraindicated in acute hepatitis (risk of AKI and bleeding from antiplatelet effects)

medicines.name: Antiemetics (Ondansetron, Metoclopramide)
medicines.dosage: Ondansetron: 4-8 mg orally or IV every 8 hours; Metoclopramide: 10 mg orally or IV every 8 hours
medicines.use_case: Nausea and vomiting in acute hepatitis preventing adequate nutrition and hydration; ondansetron preferred (safer in liver disease — metoclopramide may accumulate in severe hepatic impairment causing extrapyramidal effects)

medicines.name: Ursodeoxycholic Acid (UDCA)
medicines.dosage: 10-15 mg/kg/day in divided doses
medicines.use_case: Cholestatic hepatitis (prolonged or severe jaundice from intrahepatic cholestasis — particularly in cholestatic HAV or HAV relapsing form); improves bile flow; reduces pruritus; mild hepatoprotective properties; used in primary biliary cholangitis; may shorten duration of cholestatic hepatitis in HAV
medicines.mechanism: Hydrophilic bile acid — replaces toxic hydrophobic bile acids; protects hepatocytes from bile salt toxicity; stimulates bile secretion
medicines.note: Safe in pregnancy (unlike most other hepatic drugs); useful in cholestatic HEV in pregnancy

medicines.name: Vitamin K (Phytomenadione) — IV
medicines.dosage: 10 mg IV once daily for 3 days
medicines.use_case: Prolonged INR in acute hepatitis — correct any Vitamin K deficiency component of coagulopathy before concluding INR elevation is purely from hepatic synthetic failure; if INR corrects with Vitamin K — suggests cholestatic component or dietary deficiency; if INR does not correct — confirms hepatic synthetic failure (poor prognostic sign)
medicines.note: ALWAYS give Vitamin K when INR is elevated in acute hepatitis BEFORE concluding liver failure

medicines.name: IV N-Acetylcysteine (NAC) — For Acute Liver Failure
medicines.dosage: 150 mg/kg IV in 200mL dextrose 5% over 15-60 minutes (loading dose); then 50 mg/kg in 500mL over 4 hours; then 100 mg/kg in 1L over 16 hours (paracetamol overdose regimen); for non-paracetamol ALF: continuous infusion 150 mg/kg/day
medicines.use_case: ACUTE LIVER FAILURE from ANY CAUSE (not just paracetamol) — the King's College/ICU protocol administers IV NAC to ALL ALF patients (viral, drug-induced, HAV); improves survival in non-paracetamol ALF (O'Grady study); mechanism: replenishes glutathione stores and improves hepatic microvascular blood flow
medicines.mechanism: Precursor to glutathione (master antioxidant); reduces oxidative stress and hepatocyte death; improves hepatic and renal microvascular flow in ALF

categories.category_name: Chronic Hepatitis B — Antiviral Therapy (Nucleos/tide Analogues)
categories.purpose: Suppress HBV replication to prevent progression of fibrosis, reduce HCC risk, and prevent decompensation. Note: these drugs suppress but do not cure HBV (the intrahepatic cccDNA reservoir persists). Treatment is usually lifelong.
categories.treatment_indications: HBV DNA >2,000 IU/mL with elevated ALT and/or liver fibrosis ≥F2 on FibroScan; ANY HBV DNA with decompensated cirrhosis; HBV DNA >20,000 IU/mL with any ALT in HBeAg-positive disease; preventive (PMTCT) in pregnancy; before immunosuppressive therapy

medicines.name: Tenofovir Disoproxil Fumarate (TDF)
medicines.dosage: 300 mg once daily with food
medicines.use_case: FIRST-LINE treatment for chronic hepatitis B; preferred over entecavir in HBV/HIV coinfection (as TDF is also antiretroviral); PMTCT — from week 24-28 of pregnancy in HBeAg-positive mothers to prevent vertical transmission; most widely used HBV antiviral globally; highly effective — suppresses HBV DNA to undetectable in 95%+ by year 1; HIGH BARRIER TO RESISTANCE
medicines.mechanism: Nucleotide analogue (prodrug of tenofovir) — inhibits HBV DNA polymerase (reverse transcriptase activity); competes with natural deoxynucleotides preventing viral DNA synthesis; also active against HIV
medicines.monitoring: Renal function (creatinine, eGFR) and phosphate every 3-6 months — TDF causes proximal tubular nephrotoxicity (Fanconi syndrome) in a small proportion; bone mineral density in long-term use; if renal impairment develops — switch to TAF
side_effects: Renal tubular dysfunction (most important — Fanconi syndrome; hypophosphataemia; glycosuria without hyperglycaemia)
Bone density loss (osteopenia/osteoporosis) with long-term use
GI intolerance (nausea, diarrhoea) — usually mild and improves
Lactic acidosis (rare but serious — stop if unexplained fatigue, abdominal pain, nausea)
medicines.india_note: Generic TDF (300 mg) widely available in India at very low cost (Rs 10-20 per tablet); affordable for long-term therapy; included in NACO HIV programme and increasingly in hepatitis B treatment guidelines

medicines.name: Tenofovir Alafenamide (TAF)
medicines.dosage: 25 mg once daily with food
medicines.use_case: Chronic hepatitis B — preferred over TDF when: renal impairment (eGFR <60); osteoporosis or bone disease; elderly patients; TAF achieves higher intrahepatic drug concentrations at much lower systemic drug levels, dramatically reducing renal and bone toxicity compared to TDF; same HBV suppression efficacy as TDF
medicines.mechanism: Novel prodrug of tenofovir — more efficiently delivered to hepatocytes with 90% lower systemic tenofovir levels than TDF; same mechanism (HBV polymerase inhibition)
medicines.advantages_over_tdf: 10-fold lower plasma tenofovir levels; significantly less renal toxicity; significantly less bone density loss; comparable HBV suppression rates
side_effects: Significantly less renal and bone toxicity than TDF
medicines.cost_note: More expensive than TDF; generic versions emerging; preferred when TDF nephrotoxicity is a concern

medicines.name: Entecavir (ETV)
medicines.dosage: Treatment-naïve: 0.5 mg once daily; Lamivudine-refractory or cirrhosis: 1 mg once daily; take on empty stomach (food reduces absorption by 50%)
medicines.use_case: First-line chronic hepatitis B — preferred alternative to TDF/TAF in patients WITHOUT HIV coinfection; excellent potency; HIGH BARRIER TO RESISTANCE (lower than TDF/TAF if previously treated with lamivudine — in that case use TDF instead); approved in children >2 years
medicines.mechanism: Deoxyguanosine analogue — inhibits HBV DNA polymerase at three steps: base priming of viral DNA synthesis; reverse transcription of pregenomic RNA; DNA-dependent DNA synthesis
medicines.advantages: Very high barrier to resistance in treatment-naïve patients; excellent tolerability; once daily; no significant renal toxicity
medicines.resistance_warning: Low barrier to resistance in lamivudine-experienced patients — entecavir resistance up to 50% by year 5 in lamivudine-resistant patients; use TDF/TAF instead in this situation
side_effects: Rare: lactic acidosis (class effect of nucleosides)

medicines.name: Pegylated Interferon Alfa-2a (PegIFN-alfa-2a)
medicines.form: Subcutaneous injection (180 mcg/0.5 mL pre-filled syringe)
medicines.dosage: 180 mcg subcutaneously once weekly for 48 weeks (HBV)
medicines.use_case: Finite-duration treatment option for selected chronic HBV patients: young patients wishing to avoid lifelong oral therapy; HBeAg-positive with high ALT, low-moderate HBV DNA, non-Asian genotype; does not require lifelong therapy — fixed 48-week course; higher rate of HBeAg seroconversion and HBsAg loss than NAs in selected patients; NOT suitable for cirrhosis, psychiatric history, autoimmune disease, pregnancy, or significant comorbidities
medicines.mechanism: Immunomodulatory (stimulates innate and adaptive immune response against HBV) + direct antiviral (induces MHC expression, NK cell activation, CTL response against infected hepatocytes)
medicines.advantages: Finite treatment duration (48 weeks); higher HBsAg loss rates in selected patients; no resistance
medicines.disadvantages: Significant side effects; injections; requires monitoring; contraindicated in many patients
side_effects: Flu-like symptoms (fever, rigors, headache, myalgia — mostly first 12 hours post-injection; paracetamol before injection prevents; improves with time)
Depression and mood changes (up to 20%; SCREEN before starting; monitor closely; can be severe)
Thyroid dysfunction (4-20% — baseline and monitoring TFTs)
Retinal changes (rare — check fundus if diabetic or hypertensive)

medicines.name: Lamivudine (LAM) — Now Largely Superseded
medicines.dosage: 100 mg once daily (HBV dose)
medicines.use_case: Previously first-line HBV; now RARELY used for HBV monotherapy due to very high resistance rates (20-30% per year; >70% by 5 years); still used in some resource-limited settings where TDF/ETV not available; part of some HIV combination regimens (3TC 300 mg for HIV suppresses HBV as secondary benefit)
medicines.resistance: VERY HIGH resistance rate — not suitable for long-term HBV monotherapy; if patient on lamivudine with resistance — switch to TDF (not ETV alone)
medicines.note: If patient is already on lamivudine with undetectable HBV DNA for >12 months — can continue but consider switching to TDF or TAF for better resistance profile

categories.category_name: Hepatitis C — Direct-Acting Antivirals (DAAs) — CURATIVE TREATMENT
categories.purpose: Cure HCV infection — achieve SVR12 (Sustained Virological Response at 12 weeks post-treatment = CURE). DAAs target HCV non-structural proteins essential for viral replication. Modern pangenotypic DAA regimens achieve SVR rates >95% across all genotypes in 8-12 weeks of oral therapy with minimal side effects.
categories.treatment_indications: ALL patients with detectable HCV RNA (positive HCV RNA) should be offered treatment regardless of: fibrosis stage (even F0-F1); ALT level (even if normal); genotype; symptoms; duration of infection. Treatment priority historically given to advanced fibrosis but WHO and major guidelines now recommend treating everyone.
categories.svr_definition: SVR12 = Undetectable HCV RNA (<12-15 IU/mL) at 12 weeks after completing DAA treatment = VIROLOGICAL CURE. Once SVR12 is achieved, HCV cannot come back from the same infection (re-infection from new exposure is possible if risk behaviours continue).

medicines.name: Sofosbuvir/Velpatasvir (SOF/VEL) — Epclusa
medicines.dosage: ONE tablet once daily for 12 weeks; 24 weeks if decompensated cirrhosis (with ribavirin for 12 weeks in Child-Pugh B/C)
medicines.use_case: PANGENOTYPIC — approved for all HCV genotypes 1-6; FIRST-LINE treatment in most guidelines; particularly important in India where GT3 predominates (GT3 is effectively treated with this combination); treatment-naïve and treatment-experienced; with or without cirrhosis (compensated — 12 weeks; decompensated with ribavirin — 12-24 weeks); WHO essential medicine; excellent SVR rates (>95% GT3; >97% GT1; >95% all genotypes)
medicines.mechanism: Sofosbuvir: NS5B nucleotide inhibitor (HCV RNA-dependent RNA polymerase inhibitor — directly blocks HCV replication); Velpatasvir: pangenotypic NS5A inhibitor (NS5A is essential for HCV RNA replication and assembly); Dual mechanism from two drug classes
medicines.generic_india: Generic sofosbuvir/velpatasvir (400/100 mg) widely available in India at approximately Rs 200-400 per tablet; full 12-week course (84 tablets) costs approximately Rs 18,000-35,000 vs brand cost of >Rs 3 lakh; under PMGAM/Pradhan Mantri Jan Arogya Yojana and National Viral Hepatitis Control Programme (NVHCP) — free or subsidised at government hospitals
side_effects: Generally extremely well tolerated — considered one of the safest drug regimens ever developed
medicines.drug_interactions: Avoid with: amiodarone (risk of severe bradycardia — case reports of fatal cardiac events); rifampicin/rifabutin (significantly reduces sofosbuvir levels — avoid); carbamazepine, phenytoin, phenobarbitone (reduce sofosbuvir/velpatasvir levels); antacids (separate by 4 hours from velpatasvir); acid-suppressive drugs (omeprazole 20 mg with food; avoid high-dose PPIs)

medicines.name: Glecaprevir/Pibrentasvir (GLE/PIB) — Mavyret / Maviret
medicines.form: Tablet (100 mg glecaprevir + 40 mg pibrentasvir; 3 tablets = one dose)
medicines.dosage: 3 tablets once daily with food for 8 weeks (most treatment-naïve patients without cirrhosis); 12 weeks (compensated cirrhosis or prior treatment failure); for GT3 with cirrhosis: 16 weeks
medicines.use_case: PANGENOTYPIC — 8-week treatment duration for most patients (non-cirrhotic, treatment-naïve) — the shortest HCV treatment duration available; preferred for: patients with moderate renal impairment (eGFR 15-30); patients on dialysis; certain drug interactions precluding sofosbuvir use; GT3 patients completing prior treatment with sofosbuvir-based regimen
medicines.mechanism: Glecaprevir: NS3/4A protease inhibitor (prevents viral polyprotein cleavage); Pibrentasvir: pangenotypic NS5A inhibitor; Dual drug class mechanism
medicines.svr_rates: GT1-6: 97-99% in treatment-naïve non-cirrhotic patients; 97-98% in compensated cirrhosis
medicines.advantage_over_sofvel: 8-week treatment option; no dose adjustment for renal impairment (both drugs hepatically metabolised — safe in severe renal failure and dialysis); appropriate for GT1 treatment failures
medicines.disadvantage: Cannot be used in decompensated cirrhosis (Child-Pugh B/C); requires food with each dose; more drug interactions (protease inhibitor); 3 tablets daily

medicines.name: Sofosbuvir/Ledipasvir (SOF/LED) — Harvoni
medicines.dosage: ONE tablet once daily for 12 weeks (GT1, GT4, GT5, GT6); 8 weeks for GT1 treatment-naïve without cirrhosis and low viral load (<6 million IU/mL)
medicines.use_case: Excellent for GT1, GT4, GT5, GT6; NOT recommended for GT2 or GT3 (ledipasvir has poor activity against GT3 — use SOF/VEL instead); widely available generics in India at low cost; one of the most prescribed HCV regimens globally
