medicines.mechanism: Sofosbuvir: NS5B inhibitor; Ledipasvir: NS5A inhibitor (GT1, 4, 5, 6-specific)
medicines.india_note: Generic sofosbuvir/ledipasvir widely available in India; generic manufacturers include Natco, Cipla, Sun Pharma; NVHCP programme provides free or subsidised treatment at district hospitals

medicines.name: Sofosbuvir + Daclatasvir (SOF + DCV)
medicines.form: Two separate tablets — Sofosbuvir 400 mg once daily + Daclatasvir 60 mg once daily
medicines.dosage: Both tablets once daily for 12 weeks; 24 weeks for decompensated cirrhosis or prior treatment failure (with ribavirin consideration)
medicines.use_case: Most widely used regimen in India and many low-income countries due to very low generic cost; effective across genotypes 1, 2, 3, 4; particularly important for GT3 (the dominant genotype in India); reasonable SVR rates for GT3 (88-92%) though slightly lower than SOF/VEL for GT3
medicines.mechanism: Sofosbuvir: NS5B inhibitor; Daclatasvir: NS5A inhibitor (pangenotypic NS5A inhibition)
medicines.svr_rates: GT1: 96-98%; GT2: 96-99%; GT3: 88-92% (lower than SOF/VEL — particularly GT3 with cirrhosis); GT4: 95%
medicines.india_generic_cost: Sofosbuvir + daclatasvir generic combination costs approximately Rs 4,000-10,000 for a full 12-week course (one of the most affordable HCV regimens globally); extensively produced by Indian generic manufacturers
medicines.note: For GT3, SOF/VEL is now preferred over SOF+DCV given higher GT3 SVR rates; SOF+DCV remains important in settings where SOF/VEL is not available or affordable

medicines.name: Ribavirin (RBV) — Used in Combination (Not Monotherapy)
medicines.dosage: Weight-based: <75 kg: 1000 mg/day in divided doses; ≥75 kg: 1200 mg/day; take with food; duration depends on regimen and fibrosis
medicines.use_case: Added to DAA regimens in specific high-risk scenarios: decompensated cirrhosis (SOF/VEL + RBV for 12 weeks); GT3 with cirrhosis; prior treatment failures in difficult-to-treat patients; NS5A inhibitor failures; generally reduces relapse in difficult cases
medicines.mechanism: Guanosine nucleoside analogue — multiple mechanisms including immunomodulatory, inhibition of HCV NS5B polymerase (weak), and mutagenic effect on HCV RNA; acts as accessory drug to boost DAA effectiveness
side_effects: HAEMOLYTIC ANAEMIA — most common and important side effect; can be severe; monitor haemoglobin at 2 and 4 weeks
Teratogenicity — ABSOLUTE CONTRAINDICATION in pregnancy and men whose female partner is pregnant (requires 6 months contraception after stopping RBV)
medicines.monitoring: FBC at 2 and 4 weeks after starting (haemoglobin); reduce dose if Hb falls >2 g/dL; stop if Hb <8.5 g/dL

categories.category_name: HBV Prevention — PMTCT (Prevention of Mother-to-Child Transmission)
categories.purpose: Preventing vertical transmission of HBV from HBsAg-positive mother to neonate — the most important route of chronicity acquisition globally. Combination approach: maternal antiviral therapy in late pregnancy + neonatal HBIG + immediate HBV vaccination at birth.

medicines.name: Hepatitis B Immunoglobulin (HBIG) — Neonatal
brand_examples: HBIG — available through government programs India
medicines.form: IM injection (200 IU per mL; standard neonatal dose 100 IU/0.5 mL)
medicines.dosage: 100-200 IU IM within 12 hours of birth (ideally within 2 hours); single dose; given simultaneously with first HBV vaccine dose at different injection sites
medicines.use_case: All neonates born to HBsAg-positive mothers; passive immunisation — provides immediate protection against HBV exposure at delivery while active immunisation from HBV vaccine develops; reduces vertical transmission risk from 90% (untreated) to <5% (HBIG + vaccine); in HBeAg-positive mothers: HBIG + vaccine + maternal antiviral TDF from week 28 reduces to <1%
medicines.mechanism: Pre-formed anti-HBs antibodies provide immediate passive protection against HBV until infant mounts active immune response from HBV vaccine
medicines.india_note: HBIG + birth dose HBV vaccine now recommended under India's Universal Immunisation Programme (UIP) — availability at government hospitals improving; all deliveries should provide birth dose HBV vaccine within 24 hours

medicines.name: TDF (Tenofovir) in Pregnancy — PMTCT for High-Viral-Load Mothers
medicines.dosage: 300 mg TDF once daily from week 24-28 of pregnancy until at least 12 weeks postpartum (or delivery — depending on protocol)
medicines.use_case: HBsAg-positive pregnant women with HIGH viral load (HBV DNA >200,000 IU/mL — typically HBeAg-positive) — maternal antiviral therapy dramatically reduces peripartum viral load and vertical transmission risk; combined with HBIG + vaccine at birth reduces transmission to <1%; safe in pregnancy (FDA category B); WHO-recommended
medicines.monitoring: HBV DNA at baseline and at week 28-32; renal function; postpartum: monitor for HBV DNA flare after stopping TDF
medicines.note: Lower risk HBsAg-positive mothers (low HBV DNA, HBeAg negative) may not need maternal TDF — HBIG + vaccine alone sufficient; specialist decision

categories.purpose: Management of portal hypertension complications in decompensated cirrhosis from chronic HBV/HCV.

medicines.name: Spironolactone + Furosemide — Ascites Management
medicines.dosage: Spironolactone: 100-400 mg/day; Furosemide: 40-160 mg/day; target: weight loss 0.5 kg/day (ascites) or 1 kg/day (ascites + oedema); Na >120 mmol/L target; ratio maintained at 100:40 (spiro:furo)
medicines.use_case: First-line treatment for ascites in cirrhosis; spironolactone blocks aldosterone (elevated in cirrhosis causing Na and water retention); furosemide provides additional diuresis
medicines.monitoring: Daily weight; urine output; electrolytes (K+, Na+) every 1-2 weeks when adjusting dose; renal function; hyponatraemia (<120 mmol/L) and AKI are reasons to reduce or stop

medicines.name: Lactulose — Hepatic Encephalopathy
medicines.dosage: 30-45 mL orally 2-3 times daily; titrate to 2-4 soft stools per day
medicines.use_case: Prevention and treatment of hepatic encephalopathy in cirrhosis; lactulose is converted by colonic bacteria to lactic and acetic acids — acidifies the colon, traps ammonium (NH4+), and reduces ammonia absorption; also cathartic — decreases gut transit time reducing ammonia production; first-line therapy for overt hepatic encephalopathy
medicines.mechanism: Colonic acidification: NH3 + H+ → NH4+ (trapped, cannot be absorbed); cathartic: reduces gut transit and ammonia-producing bacteria

medicines.name: Rifaximin — Hepatic Encephalopathy (Secondary Prophylaxis)
medicines.dosage: 550 mg twice daily (hepatic encephalopathy prophylaxis)
medicines.use_case: Prevention of recurrent hepatic encephalopathy episodes in patients who have had ≥2 episodes — added to lactulose (not replacing); non-absorbable rifamycin antibiotic that reduces ammonia-producing gut bacteria; significantly reduces hospitalisation from HE recurrence (RCT evidence); better tolerated than lactulose alone
medicines.evidence: Bass et al. NEJM 2010: rifaximin significantly reduced HE recurrence vs placebo and reduced hospitalisations in cirrhotic patients

medicines.name: Terlipressin — Variceal Bleeding and Hepatorenal Syndrome
medicines.dosage: Variceal bleeding: 1-2 mg IV every 4-6 hours until bleeding controlled, then 1 mg every 4-6 hours for 5 days; Hepatorenal Syndrome type 1: 0.5-1 mg IV every 4-6 hours; titrate up to 2 mg if creatinine not improving; with IV albumin 20-40 g/day
medicines.use_case: Acute oesophageal variceal bleeding (alongside band ligation endoscopy + IV octreotide — triple therapy is standard of care); Hepatorenal Syndrome Type 1 — the only vasopressor combination with significant evidence for HRS reversal (terlipressin + albumin reversal rate 40-50%); reduces splanchnic blood flow and portal pressure
medicines.mechanism: Vasopressin V1 receptor agonist — causes splanchnic vasoconstriction reducing portal venous blood flow and pressure

medicines.name: Ceftriaxone IV — Spontaneous Bacterial Peritonitis (SBP)
medicines.dosage: 2 g IV once daily for 5 days (SBP treatment); IV albumin 1.5 g/kg on day 1 + 1 g/kg on day 3 (prevents SBP-induced AKI and HRS)
medicines.use_case: Treatment of spontaneous bacterial peritonitis; E. coli and Klebsiella pneumoniae are most common causative organisms; always give with IV albumin to prevent deterioration of renal function (SORT trial)
medicines.note: Quinolone prophylaxis: norfloxacin 400 mg once daily for secondary SBP prophylaxis

categories.purpose: Treatment of liver cancer developing as a complication of chronic HBV/HCV-related cirrhosis.

medicines.name: Sorafenib (Nexavar) — Systemic Therapy Advanced HCC
medicines.dosage: 400 mg twice daily with food; dose reduce to 400 mg once daily if toxicity
medicines.use_case: Advanced HCC (Barcelona Clinic Liver Cancer Stage C — metastatic or vascular invasion) or when local treatments (resection, ablation, TACE) have failed; first targeted therapy approved for HCC (SHARP trial); modest survival benefit (median OS 10.7 vs 7.9 months vs placebo)
medicines.mechanism: Multi-kinase inhibitor: inhibits VEGFR1/2/3, PDGFR, RAF kinases — reduces tumour angiogenesis and tumour cell proliferation
medicines.note: Largely superseded by lenvatinib (REFLECT trial — superior response rates) and atezolizumab + bevacizumab (immunotherapy combination — IMbrave150 trial — first to show OS superiority over sorafenib) in eligible patients

medicines.name: Atezolizumab + Bevacizumab (Tecentriq + Avastin) — First-Line Advanced HCC
medicines.dosage: Atezolizumab 1200 mg IV + Bevacizumab 15 mg/kg IV every 3 weeks
medicines.use_case: Advanced/unresectable HCC as first-line treatment (if no varices or recent variceal bleed — bevacizumab risk of GI bleeding; requires prior endoscopy to exclude high-risk varices); IMbrave150 trial showed superior OS and PFS vs sorafenib; standard of care in eligible patients in international guidelines
medicines.note: Expensive; access in India limited to private sector currently; patient assistance programmes available through manufacturer

medicines.name: Transarterial Chemoembolisation (TACE) — Locoregional Therapy
medicines.use_case: Intermediate-stage HCC (BCLC B) not amenable to curative resection or ablation; delivers chemotherapy (doxorubicin or cisplatin) emulsified with Lipiodol directly into hepatic artery feeding the tumour, followed by embolisation; first-line locoregional therapy for multifocal HCC
medicines.note: Not a medication per se — locoregional procedure; listed for completeness as major treatment modality

diet_and_nutrition.overview: Diet plays a critical but often underappreciated role in viral hepatitis outcomes. In ACUTE hepatitis: nutrition supports hepatocyte regeneration and immune function; adequate caloric intake is essential even when nausea and anorexia severely reduce appetite. In CHRONIC hepatitis and cirrhosis: nutrition is a life-threatening concern — malnutrition is present in 25-80% of cirrhotic patients and is an independent predictor of mortality, hospitalisation, and post-transplant outcomes. The liver is central to all metabolic processes — when it fails, nutritional requirements change dramatically. Post-SVR (after HCV cure): diet can support liver regeneration and fibrosis regression.

phase_acute_hepatitis.priority: Adequate caloric and protein intake despite profound anorexia and nausea — critical for hepatocyte regeneration and immune function
phase_acute_hepatitis.fluid_requirement: 2.5-3 litres per day; IV fluids if vomiting prevents adequate oral intake
phase_acute_hepatitis.caloric_requirement: 25-35 kcal/kg/day during acute hepatitis (hepatic inflammation increases metabolic rate by 10-20%)
phase_acute_hepatitis.protein_requirement: 1.0-1.2 g protein/kg/day (do NOT restrict protein in uncomplicated acute hepatitis — protein restriction is OUTDATED advice and harmful; only restrict in FRANK hepatic encephalopathy)
phase_acute_hepatitis.key_principle: Small, frequent meals (5-6 small meals per day); eat when appetite is best (often morning); energy-dense foods; avoid large meals that distend stomach and worsen nausea

recommended_foods.rationale: The liver regenerates hepatocytes using dietary amino acids; adequate protein intake is the most important nutritional principle in hepatitis; protein restriction for hepatitis is outdated and harmful (only restrict in frank encephalopathy)

items.benefit: Complete protein (all essential amino acids); BCAA-rich (branched-chain amino acids — leucine, isoleucine, valine — most hepatoprotective amino acids; liver uses BCAAs differently from other proteins); easily digestible; Vitamin D; selenium; lecithin (phosphatidylcholine — essential for liver cell membrane integrity and bile synthesis)
items.frequency: 1-2 eggs daily; soft-boiled, poached or scrambled (easier to digest than fried)

items.benefit: High-quality casein protein (slow-release amino acids — particularly useful as evening snack in cirrhosis to prevent overnight nitrogen catabolism — a critical nutritional strategy in advanced liver disease); calcium; phosphorus
items.frequency: Small portions twice daily in cirrhosis patients

items.food: Moong dal (Green gram), Masoor dal (Red lentils)
items.benefit: Plant protein; BCAA content; easily digestible; low in fat; fermented/sprouted moong has prebiotic benefit (reduces gut ammonia production — important in cirrhosis); folate; iron; zinc
items.frequency: Daily as dal — traditional Indian diet provides excellent hepatic nutrition

items.benefit: High biological value complete protein; low saturated fat; tryptophan and tyrosine (precursors to neurotransmitters — important in hepatic encephalopathy); omega-3 fatty acids in oily fish (anti-inflammatory)
items.frequency: 3-4 times per week; steamed, baked, or boiled — not fried

recommended_foods.rationale: Viral hepatitis involves sustained hepatic inflammation driving fibrosis; anti-inflammatory dietary compounds may slow fibrosis progression and support hepatocyte defence mechanisms

items.food: Coffee (2-3 cups of freshly brewed coffee per day)
items.benefit: STRONGEST EVIDENCE BASE of any single dietary factor for liver health; multiple large epidemiological studies (>9 prospective cohort studies) consistently show: 2-3 cups of caffeinated coffee per day associated with: 40-65% reduction in cirrhosis risk; 40-50% reduction in HCC risk; slower fibrosis progression in chronic HCV; improved response to HCV interferon-based treatment; improved outcomes in NAFLD; reduction in liver enzyme levels (ALT, GGT). Mechanisms: caffeic acid and chlorogenic acid antioxidants; caffeine reduces TGF-beta (pro-fibrotic cytokine); inhibits stellate cell activation; anti-inflammatory and antifibrotic effects
items.frequency: 2-3 cups of regular caffeinated coffee per day (not decaffeinated — benefit largely from caffeinated compounds); filter or instant coffee — both effective; avoid adding sugar and large amounts of full-fat milk
items.note: One of the most important dietary recommendations for all patients with chronic liver disease; coffee is actively hepatoprotective

items.benefit: Curcumin — inhibits NF-κB (key transcription factor for hepatic inflammatory cytokines IL-6, TNF-alpha, IL-1β); inhibits hepatic stellate cell activation (the cells that produce liver fibrosis collagen); antioxidant; anti-viral properties (curcumin inhibits HBV and HCV replication in cell culture studies); black pepper (piperine) increases curcumin bioavailability 20-fold
items.frequency: Daily in cooking; haldi doodh (turmeric golden milk); must use black pepper

items.benefit: Allicin and organosulphur compounds — hepatoprotective antioxidants; S-allylmercaptocysteine induces glutathione S-transferase (phase II detoxification enzyme); reduces oxidative stress in hepatocytes; anti-inflammatory; reduces serum cholesterol (non-alcoholic fatty liver — common coexisting condition)
items.frequency: 2-3 raw or lightly cooked cloves daily; crush and allow to rest before cooking

items.benefit: Epigallocatechin gallate (EGCG) — most studied antioxidant in liver disease; reduces hepatic lipid accumulation; anti-fibrotic (inhibits TGF-β-induced stellate cell activation); inhibits HBV and HCV replication in vitro; protects against NAFLD-related liver damage; epidemiological data: green tea consumption associated with lower HCC risk in Asian populations
items.frequency: 2-3 cups of unsweetened green tea daily
items.caution: High-dose green tea EXTRACT supplements can be hepatotoxic (paradoxically) — use tea NOT extract supplements

items.benefit: Betaine — methyl donor that protects liver cells; reduces hepatic fat accumulation; betalains (antioxidant pigments); nitrates (improve hepatic blood flow); fibre; reduces liver inflammatory markers in animal studies; commonly recommended in traditional hepatic diets
items.frequency: Daily as juice, salad, or cooked vegetable

items.benefit: Silymarin (mixture of flavonolignans — silibinin, silidianin, silicristin) is the most extensively studied natural hepatoprotective compound; antioxidant; anti-inflammatory; anti-fibrotic (inhibits stellate cell activation and collagen synthesis); membrane-stabilising (prevents hepatotoxin entry into hepatocytes); used as adjunct in alcoholic and drug-induced hepatitis; some small studies show reduction in ALT in chronic HBV; IV silibinin is approved treatment for Amanita mushroom (death cap) poisoning
items.evidence: Cochrane review: insufficient evidence for silymarin in viral hepatitis specifically; widely used as complementary therapy; no major safety concerns at standard doses; AVOID in pregnancy
items.frequency: Silymarin 140-200 mg three times daily (standardised extract) as adjunct; widely available in India as Silymarin / Legalon / Silybon
items.note: Not a replacement for antiviral therapy — an adjunct only

recommended_foods.category: High-Antioxidant Foods (Combat Oxidative Stress in Viral Hepatitis)
recommended_foods.rationale: Hepatitis viruses and the immune response they generate create massive oxidative stress in hepatocytes — overwhelming the liver's antioxidant defences (glutathione, superoxide dismutase, catalase); dietary antioxidants supplement these depleted defences

items.benefit: 600-900 mg Vitamin C per 100g (richest Vitamin C food); tannins, ellagic acid, gallic acid; powerful free radical scavenger; regenerates Vitamin E (the primary fat-soluble antioxidant protecting hepatocyte membranes); reduces hepatic oxidative stress markers; enhances liver detoxification (induces glutathione-S-transferase); traditional Ayurvedic hepatoprotective herb with strong scientific basis
items.frequency: 1-3 amla daily; amla murabba, raw, or juice

items.benefit: Punicalagins (the most potent antioxidant polyphenols known — 3× more antioxidant capacity than red wine and green tea combined); ellagic acid (hepatoprotective, anti-fibrotic); reduces hepatic inflammation markers (CRP, IL-6) in clinical studies
items.frequency: 1 pomegranate or glass of fresh pomegranate juice daily

items.benefit: Papain enzyme (aids protein digestion — helpful when hepatic bile flow reduced); Vitamin C and beta-carotene (antioxidants); potassium; lycopene; gently improves liver function markers in some studies

Omega-3 fatty acids (ALA — anti-inflammatory); arginine (precursor to nitric oxide — reduces ammonia; useful in hepatic encephalopathy); glutathione (direct antioxidant); polyphenols; magnesium; reduces liver fat and inflammation in NAFLD

recommended_foods.category: Evening Snack — Critical for Cirrhosis (Nocturnal Nutritional Support)
recommended_foods.rationale: Patients with cirrhosis have a very short overnight fasting tolerance — their glycogen stores are depleted by liver failure, and they switch to protein catabolism (breaking down muscle for energy) within 4-6 hours of fasting. A LATE EVENING SNACK (200-300 kcal, carbohydrate + protein) immediately before sleep is one of the single most evidence-based nutritional interventions in cirrhosis — it reduces overnight muscle catabolism and improves nitrogen balance

items.food: Late evening snack for cirrhosis (200-300 kcal)
items.examples: Warm milk with honey + 2 biscuits; small bowl of oats; paneer sandwich; small portion of rice with dal; banana + peanut butter; BCAA supplement + light carbohydrate
items.benefit: Prevents overnight protein catabolism (a major contributor to the sarcopenia/muscle wasting of cirrhosis); improves nitrogen balance; reduces fasting hypoglycaemia risk; evidence: late evening snack significantly improves nutritional status and quality of life in cirrhotic patients
items.frequency: EVERY NIGHT for all cirrhotic patients — within 30-60 minutes of going to bed

foods_to_strictly_avoid.reason: The single most important dietary restriction in ALL viral hepatitis: acute hepatitis, chronic hepatitis, and post-SVR. Alcohol and viral hepatitis act SYNERGISTICALLY — each doubles the other's liver-damaging effect. Alcohol causes: direct hepatotoxicity (acetaldehyde — the toxic metabolite) impairing hepatocyte DNA repair; increased intestinal permeability to bacterial endotoxin (LPS — a major driver of hepatic inflammation); activation of hepatic stellate cells (fibrosis-producing cells); oxidative stress depletion of glutathione; suppression of innate and adaptive immune responses against HBV/HCV; dramatically accelerated fibrosis progression (3-5× faster in heavy drinkers with chronic hepatitis). In cirrhosis: ANY alcohol dramatically increases risk of variceal bleeding, hepatic decompensation, and HCC. SVR (HCV cure) does not restore safe drinking — the liver damage from fibrosis and the cirrhosis risk persist; alcohol remains harmful.
foods_to_strictly_avoid.duration: LIFETIME ABSTINENCE for all patients with cirrhosis; complete abstinence during any acute hepatitis and throughout antiviral treatment; strong recommendation for complete abstinence in all chronic HBV/HCV
foods_to_strictly_avoid.examples: Beer, wine, spirits, toddy/arrack, sharab — ALL forms of alcohol; no 'safe' level

foods_to_strictly_avoid.reason: Filter-feeding shellfish concentrate pathogens from polluted water — including HAV, HEV, Vibrio vulnificus, and other pathogens; raw shellfish are a major source of HAV and HEV in endemic areas. In cirrhotic patients: Vibrio vulnificus (bacteria in raw seafood) causes RAPIDLY FATAL septicaemia in patients with liver disease — mortality >50% within 48 hours; cirrhotic patients are severely immunocompromised and cannot fight Vibrio infections; this is a life-threatening prohibition for ALL cirrhotics
foods_to_strictly_avoid.examples: Raw oysters, uncooked mussels, clams, raw prawns, crab
foods_to_strictly_avoid.duration: Lifetime prohibition for cirrhosis; avoid during acute hepatitis; cook shellfish thoroughly (steam until all shells open + 5 minutes more)

foods_to_strictly_avoid.food: Herbal Medicines and Unlicensed Supplements with Hepatotoxic Potential
foods_to_strictly_avoid.reason: Drug-induced liver injury (DILI) is increasingly common from herbal, Ayurvedic, and traditional medicines — and can be catastrophic in patients with pre-existing hepatitis. The liver processes all substances — a compromised liver is at much higher risk of drug-toxicity. Known hepatotoxic Ayurvedic and herbal preparations: Kalihari/Jangli methi; Shankhpushpi (some preparations); Kutki; certain metal-containing preparations (bhasmas); Kava kava; comfrey; pyrrolizidine alkaloids; Chapparal; pennyroyal
examples: Certain Ayurvedic preparations containing heavy metals (mercury — parad; lead — shishe ka safeda; copper)
foods_to_strictly_avoid.recommendation: Disclose ALL herbal, traditional, and complementary medicines to your hepatologist; do not assume 'natural' = safe; many Ayurvedic preparations are hepatoprotective and appropriate (amla, turmeric) but some are seriously hepatotoxic

foods_to_strictly_avoid.food: Excessive Sodium (Salt) — Critical for Ascites Management in Cirrhosis
foods_to_strictly_avoid.reason: Cirrhosis with portal hypertension causes renal sodium retention (via activated renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system and sympathetic nervous system) — excess dietary sodium directly worsens ascites accumulation and oedema; also increases risk of hyponatraemia complications
foods_to_strictly_avoid.recommendation: Sodium restriction <2 g/day (88 mmol/day) in patients with ascites — this is the amount that allows diuretics to achieve a negative sodium balance and reduce ascites; use herbs and spices for flavouring instead of salt; avoid processed foods, pickles, papads, and packaged sauces (extremely high sodium)
foods_to_strictly_avoid.note: Strict sodium restriction ONLY in patients with active ascites; not necessary in compensated cirrhosis without ascites

foods_to_strictly_avoid.reason: Liver is central to lipid metabolism — chronic hepatitis impairs hepatic fat processing; fatty liver (hepatic steatosis) commonly coexists with HCV (particularly GT3) and accelerates fibrosis; dietary fat overload worsens hepatic steatosis, increases oxidative stress, and impairs hepatocyte regeneration
foods_to_strictly_avoid.examples: Deep-fried foods; full-fat dairy in excess; processed meats; fast food; high-fat pastries
foods_to_strictly_avoid.recommendation: Replace with lean protein, olive oil, and healthy fats (nuts, avocado)

foods_to_strictly_avoid.food: Excess Red Meat and Processed Meats
foods_to_strictly_avoid.reason: High haem iron from red meat promotes oxidative stress (iron catalyses Fenton reaction generating hydroxyl radicals — highly hepatotoxic); elevated serum ferritin and hepatic iron are common in HCV and worsen fibrosis; dietary iron overload impairs interferon response in HCV; nitrosamines in processed meats are hepatocarcinogens
foods_to_strictly_avoid.recommendation: Moderate red meat (1-2 times per week); avoid processed/cured meats (ham, salami, sausages); prefer lean white meat and fish

acute_hepatitis.principle: Small frequent meals; easily digestible; high-quality protein; adequate calories despite anorexia; NO alcohol; NO hepatotoxic medications
acute_hepatitis.early_morning: Warm water with honey and lemon; 1-2 fresh amla (Vitamin C)
acute_hepatitis.breakfast: Soft scrambled eggs (2) + plain white toast; OR moong dal khichdi (very soft, minimal spice); 1 glass of diluted fruit juice; weak tea
acute_hepatitis.lunch: Plain rice + moong dal + boiled or steamed vegetable; small portion curd (probiotic); small glass of pomegranate juice
acute_hepatitis.afternoon: Warm milk with turmeric + small biscuits; amla juice
acute_hepatitis.dinner: Chicken or fish soup; plain khichdi; steamed vegetables; 1 glass of warm water
acute_hepatitis.bedtime: Warm haldi doodh (turmeric milk); no food within 2 hours of sleep
acute_hepatitis.avoid_completely: All alcohol, raw shellfish, fried food, spicy food, large portions, hepatotoxic herbs

chronic_hepatitis_compensated.principle: Mediterranean-style diet; high protein; coffee daily; complete alcohol abstinence; liver-supporting foods
chronic_hepatitis_compensated.on_waking: 2 cups of black coffee (strong evidence for hepatoprotection); 1-2 amla
chronic_hepatitis_compensated.breakfast: Eggs (2) + whole grain toast + avocado; OR oats with walnuts and berries
chronic_hepatitis_compensated.lunch: Dal + brown rice + cooked vegetables with haldi; curd; salad; green tea
chronic_hepatitis_compensated.afternoon: Green tea; 1 cup of coffee; fruit (papaya or guava)
chronic_hepatitis_compensated.dinner: Fish or chicken + dal + sabzi; roti or light rice
chronic_hepatitis_compensated.evening_snack_cirrhosis: 200 kcal evening snack before bed: warm milk + small bowl oats; CRITICAL for cirrhosis patients

alcohol_cessation.overview: ABSOLUTE ALCOHOL ABSTINENCE is the single most important lifestyle modification for all patients with any form of viral hepatitis. This cannot be overstated.
strategies: Brief motivational intervention at every consultation (5 A's: Ask, Advise, Assess, Assist, Arrange)
Referral to alcohol cessation programme (Alcoholics Anonymous, CBT-based addiction counselling)
Pharmacotherapy for alcohol dependence: naltrexone 50 mg daily; acamprosate 666 mg three times daily — both reduce craving; discuss with hepatologist (hepatic safety considerations)
Baclofen (GABA-B agonist) — one of the only anti-craving medications with evidence of safety in cirrhosis (Addolorato et al., Lancet 2007)
In-patient alcohol rehabilitation if severe dependence

hav_prevention: HAV vaccination — 2-dose series; provides >95% protection for life after both doses; recommended for all travellers to endemic areas, food handlers, people with chronic liver disease (higher risk of fulminant HAV), MSM, household contacts of HAV cases
Safe water and food practices — boil drinking water in endemic areas; avoid raw shellfish; 'boil it, cook it, peel it, or forget it' for travel
Meticulous handwashing with soap for ≥20 seconds after toilet and before food preparation
Food handlers with HAV must be excluded from work until 7 days after jaundice onset
hbv_prevention: HBV vaccination — 3-dose series (0, 1, 6 months); check anti-HBs titre 4-8 weeks after completing series; >10 mIU/mL = protected; non-responders may need booster or double-dose schedule; vaccinate ALL non-immune household and sexual contacts of HBsAg-positive patients
Safe sex — condoms reduce but do not eliminate HBV transmission; discuss with HBsAg-positive patients that they should inform sexual partners and vaccinate them
Birth-dose HBV vaccine — within 24 hours of birth for ALL neonates (India UIP); HBIG for neonates born to HBsAg-positive mothers
Universal blood screening — all donated blood in India screened for HBsAg (mandatory since 2001)
Safe injection practices — single-use syringes; do not share any injection equipment
Healthcare worker protection — HBV vaccination is mandatory for all healthcare workers in India; report all needlestick injuries; post-exposure prophylaxis (HBIG + vaccination) within 24-48 hours
Do not share personal items — razors, toothbrushes, nail clippers — items potentially contaminated with blood
In India: barber shop razors should be single-use or sterilised — significant transmission route
hcv_prevention: No vaccine exists for HCV — all prevention is behavioural and harm reduction
Harm reduction for PWID: needle and syringe programmes (NSP); opioid substitution therapy (OST — methadone, buprenorphine); naloxone availability; non-judgemental healthcare access
Safe injection practices in healthcare: single-use syringes and needles in ALL settings; never reuse; safe disposal of sharps
Universal blood screening — HCV antibody screening of all donated blood and organs since 1992 in most countries; NAT (nucleic acid testing) further reduces window period risk
Caution with tattooing, piercing, acupuncture — only use sterile single-use equipment
Barber shop practices — single-use razors in India; major HCV transmission route

Safe sex — though HCV sexual transmission is less efficient than HBV; consistent condom use in MSM (higher transmission risk) and multiple partners; HIV-coinfected patients: higher sexual HCV transmission — use condoms
HCV-positive patients on DAA treatment: still use transmission precautions until SVR confirmed (HCV RNA undetectable)

hcc_surveillance_and_monitoring.overview: Regular HCC surveillance is one of the most important ongoing management tasks for all patients with chronic HBV (especially with cirrhosis, family history of HCC, or high viral load) and all patients with HCV-related cirrhosis (even post-SVR — cirrhosis persists after viral cure and HCC risk, though reduced, remains elevated for life).
protocol: Liver ultrasound every 6 months — essential; continues lifelong once cirrhosis established
AFP (alpha-fetoprotein) every 6 months — alongside ultrasound; though non-specific, combined with ultrasound improves early HCC detection
Any new liver lesion >1 cm on ultrasound — multiphasic contrast CT or MRI for characterisation (LI-RADS scoring system)
Post-SVR HCV: continue 6-monthly surveillance INDEFINITELY for patients with established cirrhosis — HCC risk reduced after SVR but NOT eliminated
Post-TDF/ETV for HBV: continue surveillance — virus suppressed but cccDNA and integrated viral DNA persist as carcinogens

weight_and_metabolic_management: Obesity and type 2 diabetes dramatically worsen fibrosis progression in HCV (particularly GT3) and HBV — metabolic syndrome co-existing with viral hepatitis acts synergistically; every 1 unit increase in BMI increases HCC risk by 17% in HBV
Target BMI 18.5-25 kg/m2; waist circumference <90 cm men, <80 cm women
Regular aerobic exercise: 150 minutes/week moderate intensity — reduces hepatic steatosis, systemic inflammation, and insulin resistance

Treat diabetes and dyslipidaemia: HbA1c target <7% in diabetic HBV/HCV patients; metformin may be hepatoprotective in HCV + diabetes (reduces fibrosis and HCC risk); statins — generally safe in well-compensated chronic hepatitis and reduce HCC risk (emerging evidence)
Treat NAFLD/NASH coexisting with viral hepatitis — extremely important as NASH + viral hepatitis accelerates cirrhosis dramatically
mental_health_support: Depression, anxiety, and cognitive impairment are significantly more prevalent in patients with chronic HCV (direct viral neuropsychiatric effects, independent of liver disease); depression prevalence up to 30-40% in chronic HCV

HCV cure (SVR) improves depression, fatigue, and quality of life significantly — this was a major limitation of interferon-based therapy (interferon caused/worsened depression) that no longer applies to DAA therapy
Screen all chronic HBV and HCV patients for depression — PHQ-9; refer for counselling and SSRIs if needed (SSRIs generally safe in compensated hepatitis)

Stigma: both HBV and HCV carry significant social stigma (association with IV drug use, sexual transmission) — non-judgemental, confidential care is essential; stigma is a major barrier to testing and treatment
Disclosure: support patients in discussing diagnosis with partners (important for HBV sexual transmission prevention); counselling on who to tell and how

hepatitis_monitoring_plan.note: Monitoring requirements vary dramatically between acute hepatitis (weeks), treated and cured HCV (years of post-SVR follow-up), and lifelong chronic HBV management. This guide provides a framework.

green_zone.criteria: INR normal (<1.3); bilirubin elevated but improving; ALT elevated but not >1000 U/L; no confusion; able to eat and drink; SpO2 and haemodynamics normal
green_zone.action: Weekly LFTs, INR, bilirubin; urine colour monitoring daily (darkening = worsening); advise return immediately if confusion develops, INR rises, or vomiting prevents hydration; complete alcohol abstinence; no paracetamol >1g/day; no NSAIDs

yellow_zone.criteria: INR 1.2-1.5 (early coagulopathy); severe vomiting; bilirubin rapidly rising; inability to maintain oral hydration; significant prodrome with prostration
yellow_zone.action: Hospital admission; daily LFTs, INR, bilirubin, renal function, blood glucose; IV fluids + antiemetics; Vitamin K IV for elevated INR; hepatology review; transplant centre alert if INR rising

criteria: INR >1.5 with ANY confusion or altered consciousness
Rapid mental deterioration — confusion, agitation, inappropriate behaviour
Deeply icteric with deteriorating clinical course
red_zone.action: IMMEDIATE hospital admission and hepatology/liver transplant centre contact; IV NAC; contact nearest liver transplant centre for assessment; patient may need emergency transfer

chronic_hbv_monitoring.treatment_monitoring: HBV DNA every 3 months until undetectable, then 6-monthly; ALT every 3 months; renal function and phosphate (if on TDF) every 3-6 months; annual FibroScan; 6-monthly AFP + ultrasound (HCC surveillance in cirrhosis)
chronic_hbv_monitoring.inactive_carrier_monitoring: HBsAg, HBV DNA, ALT every 6-12 months; 6-monthly ultrasound + AFP if cirrhosis; watch for reactivation if immunosuppression planned

chronic_hcv_monitoring.during_treatment: HCV RNA at baseline; week 4 (optional — confirms rapid virological response); end of treatment (EOT); 12 weeks post-EOT = SVR12 = CURE
chronic_hcv_monitoring.post_svr: SVR12 confirmed (undetectable HCV RNA) = CURED; LFTs at 6-monthly (should normalise); continued 6-monthly AFP + ultrasound if cirrhosis (indefinite); annual FibroScan to monitor fibrosis regression; retest HCV RNA if new exposure risk behaviour (HCV re-infection possible after SVR)

complications.description: Life-threatening complication of acute viral hepatitis — INR ≥1.5 + hepatic encephalopathy in a person without prior liver disease. Most common causes in viral hepatitis: HAV in elderly or those with pre-existing liver disease; HBV (particularly HDV superinfection); rarely HEV in pregnancy. Carries 20-40% mortality without liver transplantation.
complications.management: ICU; IV NAC; urgent liver transplant listing; treat cerebral oedema; IV glucose for hypoglycaemia; broad-spectrum antibiotics; renal support

complications.description: The end-result of years of hepatic inflammation and fibrosis — replacement of normal liver tissue with scar tissue (collagen) and regenerative nodules. Portal hypertension develops from increased resistance to portal blood flow through the scarred liver. Cirrhosis from HBV affects 15-40% of untreated chronic HBV patients over 25 years; from HCV: ~30% within 20 years. Cirrhosis from HCV may REGRESS after SVR — unique among chronic liver diseases.
complications.severity: Severe — major impact on life expectancy and quality of life
complications.management: Treat underlying virus (TDF/TAF/ETV for HBV; DAAs for HCV — fibrosis regression possible post-SVR); manage portal hypertension complications; HCC surveillance; liver transplant for decompensated disease

complications.description: Primary liver cancer — the most feared long-term complication of chronic viral hepatitis. HBV and HCV combined cause 80% of HCC globally. HBV-related HCC is unique in that it can occur even WITHOUT cirrhosis — HBV DNA integrates into the host genome and can directly activate oncogenes. HCV-related HCC occurs almost exclusively in the setting of cirrhosis. Annual HCC incidence in HBV cirrhosis: 3-8%; in HCV cirrhosis: 1-4%. Prognosis depends entirely on stage at detection — early HCC (BCLC 0/A) is curable; advanced HCC (BCLC C/D) has median survival <12 months.
complications.severity: Often fatal — the leading cancer killer globally
complications.management: Surveillance: 6-monthly ultrasound + AFP in all at-risk patients; Early detection: curative options (hepatic resection, liver transplant, radiofrequency ablation); Intermediate: TACE; Advanced: atezolizumab + bevacizumab or sorafenib/lenvatinib

complications.description: Elevated pressure in the portal venous system from cirrhosis causing: oesophageal and gastric varices (dilated vessels at gastro-oesophageal junction from portal-systemic collaterals); variceal haemorrhage (sudden, massive, life-threatening upper GI bleeding from variceal rupture — mortality 15-25% per episode); splenomegaly and hypersplenism; caput medusae.
complications.management: Non-selective beta-blockers (propranolol, carvedilol) for primary and secondary variceal prophylaxis — reduce portal pressure; endoscopic variceal band ligation; acute variceal bleeding: terlipressin + band ligation + prophylactic ceftriaxone; TIPSS (transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt) for refractory variceal bleeding

complications.description: Ascites (fluid in peritoneal cavity) is the most common complication of cirrhotic decompensation. SBP (infection of ascitic fluid without a surgical source) occurs in 10-30% of cirrhotic patients per year and is life-threatening (in-hospital mortality 20-30%). Presents as fever, abdominal pain and tenderness, and deteriorating hepatic or renal function in a patient with ascites.
complications.management: Ascites: salt restriction (<2g/day) + spironolactone + furosemide; large-volume paracentesis + IV albumin for tense ascites; SBP: IV cefotaxime + IV albumin 1.5 g/kg day 1 + 1 g/kg day 3; norfloxacin prophylaxis for secondary prevention

complications.description: Neuropsychiatric dysfunction in cirrhosis from accumulation of ammonia (and other neurotoxins not cleared by failing liver). Ranges from minimal HE (subtle cognitive impairment detectable only on testing) to overt HE (confusion, agitation, asterixis — grades 1-4) to coma (grade 4). Precipitants: GI bleeding (increases protein load); constipation; infection; electrolyte disturbances (hyponatraemia, hypokalaemia); sedatives/opioids; excessive protein intake.
complications.management: Identify and treat precipitant; lactulose (2-4 soft stools/day); rifaximin 550 mg twice daily (secondary prophylaxis); BCAA supplements; correct hyponatraemia cautiously; avoid sedatives

complications.description: Reactivation of previously suppressed or even resolved HBV in patients undergoing immunosuppression (chemotherapy, biologics such as anti-CD20 [rituximab], anti-TNF agents, corticosteroids, solid organ transplantation, haematological stem cell transplantation, HIV/AIDS). HBV reactivation can be severe or fulminant — potentially fatal. Risk is highest with anti-CD20 agents (rituximab — >40% reactivation in HBsAg-positive patients without prophylaxis).
complications.prevention: Screen ALL patients for HBsAg AND anti-HBc before any immunosuppressive therapy; HBsAg positive: start prophylactic TDF or entecavir before immunosuppression and continue for at least 6-12 months after stopping; anti-HBc positive (resolved HBV): monitor HBV DNA every 1-3 months during immunosuppression or give prophylactic antiviral; NEVER overlook HBV reactivation screening before immunosuppression

hav: Acute HAV in pregnancy: self-limiting in most; slightly higher risk of preterm labour from fever and dehydration; HAV vaccine safe in pregnancy (inactivated); recommended for susceptible pregnant travellers to endemic areas; post-exposure prophylaxis: HAV vaccine or IGIM within 2 weeks of exposure
hbv: HBV in pregnancy: one of the most critical settings — vertical transmission is the primary driver of global HBV chronicity; perinatal transmission rate: 70-90% for HBeAg-positive mothers without intervention; reduced to <5% with HBIG + vaccine; reduced to <1% with maternal TDF + HBIG + vaccine
Screen ALL pregnant women for HBsAg at first antenatal visit — mandatory under NACO India guidelines
If HBsAg positive: test HBeAg, HBV DNA, LFTs; refer to hepatologist; PMTCT protocol
TDF (300 mg daily) from week 24-28 in HBeAg-positive or HBV DNA >200,000 IU/mL mothers — reduces perinatal transmission
Neonatal HBIG (100-200 IU IM) + HBV vaccine (first dose) within 12 hours of birth — regardless of maternal status (all HBsAg-positive mothers)
Complete 3-dose HBV vaccine series in neonate; test infant for HBsAg and anti-HBs at 9-12 months to confirm successful prophylaxis

Breastfeeding: SAFE for HBsAg-positive mothers if neonate received HBIG + vaccine at birth — no additional HBV transmission risk from breastfeeding; continue TDF during breastfeeding if maternal antiviral therapy indicated
hcv: HCV in pregnancy: 5-10% vertical transmission risk; no preventive intervention currently available (no HCVIG equivalent); caesarean section does NOT reduce transmission risk; breastfeeding: safe (no additional transmission risk unless nipples cracked/bleeding)
Screen ALL pregnant women for anti-HCV at first antenatal visit in high-prevalence settings (India) or in high-risk women
DAA therapy in pregnancy: currently NOT recommended — insufficient safety data in humans; treat before pregnancy (SVR reduces vertical transmission risk); treat after delivery

Infants born to HCV-positive mothers: test HCV RNA at 2 months (not antibody — maternal antibodies persist up to 18 months confounding interpretation) or anti-HCV at 18 months; if positive — refer to paediatric hepatologist; DAA therapy available for children ≥3 years in some guidelines
hev: HEV in pregnancy: HIGHEST RISK — case fatality rate 20-25% in third trimester (vs <0.5% in non-pregnant adults); causes fulminant hepatitis, DIC, preterm birth, foetal loss
Any pregnant woman with acute hepatitis of unknown cause — test HEV IgM as first priority in India; HEV is the most common cause of acute hepatitis in India
Hospitalise all pregnant women with HEV immediately; ICU if fulminant; obstetric monitoring; IV fluids; supportive care; consider ribavirin (limited data but being used in severe cases)

key_points: HAV in children under 6: typically ASYMPTOMATIC — important as children become silent reservoir spreading HAV to adults; anicteric HAV in children is one of the reasons HAV is endemic in communities

Congenital/perinatal HBV: PMTCT is the most important intervention; children with perinatally acquired HBV typically enter the immune tolerant phase (high viral load, normal ALT) for 2-3 decades before developing immune-active hepatitis

Childhood HBV vaccination: Universal HBV vaccination of ALL infants from birth is the most important global HBV control strategy; India's UIP includes HBV vaccine at birth, 6 weeks, 10 weeks, and 14 weeks; in birth-dose HBV vaccination programmes: chronic HBV rates in children drop from 8-15% to <1% within one generation

HCV in children: usually asymptomatic; DAA therapy approved for children ≥3 years (sofosbuvir/ledipasvir; glecaprevir/pibrentasvir for ≥3 years; sofosbuvir/velpatasvir emerging); treat all children with confirmed HCV RNA positive
Cholestatic HAV in children: more common than adults; jaundice more prolonged; entirely self-limiting

Neonatal hepatitis: neonatal HBV — important cause of neonatal jaundice in endemic areas; GBS hepatitis; CMV; herpes simplex hepatitis — different from community-acquired adult hepatitis; require different investigations

HIV/HBV coinfection: 5-10% of HIV patients in India have chronic HBV; HIV dramatically worsens HBV outcomes (faster fibrosis, higher HCC risk, higher mortality); FIRST-LINE ART for HIV/HBV coinfection: TDF/FTC + dolutegravir (tenofovir covers both HIV and HBV simultaneously) — MUST NOT use HBV therapy without covering HIV; HBV monotherapy with entecavir or TDF alone in HIV-coinfected patients selects HIV resistance

HIV/HCV coinfection: HIV accelerates HCV fibrosis 2-3× faster; treat HCV with DAAs regardless of HIV status; DAA interactions with HIV antiretrovirals important — check specific combinations; most modern ART (dolutegravir-based) has no significant DAA interactions; avoid regimens containing ritonavir/cobicistat with certain DAAs (check interactions); SVR rates with DAAs are equivalent to HIV-negative patients
HIV-coinfected patients with HBV should never stop TDF abruptly — risk of severe HBV reactivation and fulminant hepatitis

Haemodialysis patients have very high HBV and HCV prevalence historically (blood exposure at dialysis); universal screening before dialysis initiation; HBsAg-positive patients on dedicated dialysis machines in some centres
HBV in dialysis: entecavir preferred over TDF (TDF nephrotoxic — avoid in eGFR <30; if TDF used: dose adjustment required); TAF can be used with dose adjustment

HCV in dialysis: glecaprevir/pibrentasvir PREFERRED for dialysis patients — no sofosbuvir (renally cleared; significant accumulation at eGFR <30); full standard doses of GLE/PIB — no renal dose adjustment needed; SVR rates equivalent to non-dialysis patients; HCV cure reduces cardiovascular and mortality risk in dialysis patients

Liver transplantation for HBV: long-term antiviral therapy (TDF or entecavir) post-transplant; HBIG (anti-HBs immunoglobulin) infusions in high-risk period; HBV-DNA must be undetectable at transplant; HBsAg-positive donors to HBsAg-negative recipients possible with antiviral prophylaxis

Liver transplantation for HCV: pre-transplant DAA therapy if decompensation not too advanced (Child-Pugh <12); post-transplant DAA therapy achieves SVR in >95%; SVR significantly reduces graft fibrosis progression and graft loss; HCV-positive donor organs to HCV-negative recipients now used in USA (with immediate post-transplant DAA treatment) to expand organ supply

HBV reactivation in cancer chemotherapy: see complication section; prophylactic TDF or entecavir throughout chemotherapy and 12 months after in HBsAg-positive patients; monitor HBV DNA in anti-HBc-positive patients

vaccinations_recommended.frequency: 2-dose series: dose 1 (0 months) + dose 2 (6-18 months later); lifelong protection after 2 doses (>95% efficacy)
vaccinations_recommended.reason: HAV is the most common cause of acute viral hepatitis in India — intermediate-to-high endemic country with seasonal outbreaks during monsoon. HAV vaccination provides complete, lifelong protection. Particularly critical for: people with chronic HBV or HCV (superimposed HAV can cause fulminant hepatitis with >50% mortality in cirrhotic patients — HAV vaccination is urgently recommended for ALL patients with chronic liver disease); international travellers; food handlers; healthcare workers; MSM; household contacts of HAV cases.
vaccinations_recommended.brands_india: Havrix (GlaxoSmithKline); Avaxim (Sanofi); Vaqta (MSD); combination hepatitis A+B vaccine (Twinrix — single series covering both); combination typhoid+hepatitis A (Vivaxim/Hepatyrix)
vaccinations_recommended.india_note: HAV vaccination is NOT in India's UIP for children — available privately; cost approximately Rs 1,000-1,500 per dose; 2-dose series essential; not yet routinely given

vaccinations_recommended.frequency: Standard series: 3 doses (0, 1, 6 months); accelerated: 0, 1, 2 months (complete faster) with booster at 12 months; rapid: 0, 7 days, 21 days + booster at 12 months (for urgent need — travel, exposure); check anti-HBs titre 4-8 weeks after completing series — >10 mIU/mL = protected
vaccinations_recommended.reason: Hepatitis B vaccine is one of the most effective vaccines ever developed — 95%+ protective efficacy; provides lifelong protection in most vaccinated individuals; the primary prevention strategy for HBV. Recommended for: ALL unvaccinated infants (birth dose mandatory in India UIP — critical for PMTCT); all unvaccinated adults; healthcare workers (mandatory in India); household and sexual contacts of HBsAg-positive patients; PWID; MSM; haemodialysis patients; pre-transplant patients; people with chronic liver disease from any cause.
vaccinations_recommended.brands_india: Engerix-B (GlaxoSmithKline); Shanvac-B (Shantha Biotechnics); BEVAC; Biovac-B; Recombivax HB; Twinrix (combined A+B)
vaccinations_recommended.non_responders: 5-10% of vaccinees do not respond (non-responders — anti-HBs <10 mIU/mL): check immunocompromise status; repeat 3-dose series; double-dose regimen (40 mcg vs standard 20 mcg); consider referral for specialist management; non-responders: if anti-HBc negative (never infected) — at-risk and cannot be protected by vaccine; use barrier contraception and safe practices
vaccinations_recommended.india_upa: Birth dose HBV vaccine (within 24 hours of birth) is mandatory under India's Universal Immunisation Programme since 2011; 3 further doses at 6, 10, 14 weeks (pentavalent vaccine); dramatically reducing childhood HBV in vaccinated cohorts

vaccinations_recommended.vaccine: Hepatitis B Vaccine — Boosters and Special Groups
vaccinations_recommended.haemodialysis: Higher doses required (40 mcg per dose vs standard 20 mcg; 4-dose series); anti-HBs monitoring annually (dialysis patients lose immunity faster); booster if anti-HBs falls <10 mIU/mL
vaccinations_recommended.healthcare_workers: All healthcare workers must be vaccinated against HBV under MOHFW India guidelines; post-vaccination titre check mandatory; post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) protocol for needlestick injury
vaccinations_recommended.immunocompromised: Higher doses; 4-dose series; anti-HBs monitoring; may need repeated boosters

vaccinations_recommended.frequency: 3 doses: 0, 1, 6 months; or accelerated: 0, 7, 21 days + booster at 12 months
vaccinations_recommended.reason: Practical combined vaccine providing protection against both HAV and HBV in a single series — highly recommended for: adults being vaccinated for the first time (convenience); international travellers; patients with chronic liver disease (needs protection from both); healthcare workers

Patients with chronic hepatitis B or C have increased susceptibility to severe infections; influenza causing decompensation of cirrhosis or hepatic encephalopathy; annual influenza vaccination recommended for all patients with cirrhosis, chronic HBV, and chronic HCV
vaccinations_recommended.recommendation: Annually before flu season for all cirrhotic patients and all chronic viral hepatitis patients

frequently_asked_questions.question: What is the difference between Hepatitis A, B, and C?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: All three cause liver inflammation but are entirely different diseases: Hepatitis A (HAV) is a short-term, self-limiting infection spread through contaminated food and water (like typhoid); it always resolves completely and never becomes chronic; it is vaccine-preventable. Hepatitis B (HBV) spreads through blood, sex, and from mother to child at birth; most adults clear it within 6 months but 5-10% develop chronic infection leading to cirrhosis and liver cancer over decades; it is vaccine-preventable. Hepatitis C (HCV) spreads almost exclusively through blood (needle sharing, unscreened transfusions, contaminated medical equipment); 75-85% develop chronic infection; there is no vaccine — but it is now completely CURABLE in over 95% of patients with an 8-12 week course of oral tablets. The key differences: route of transmission; whether chronic disease develops; vaccine availability; and curability.

frequently_asked_questions.question: Hepatitis C is curable? Really? What treatment is available and how much does it cost in India?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: Yes — completely curable. The development of direct-acting antiviral (DAA) medicines in the last decade has transformed hepatitis C from a difficult-to-treat lifelong infection into a curable disease. Modern DAA regimens (sofosbuvir/velpatasvir, sofosbuvir + daclatasvir, or glecaprevir/pibrentasvir) achieve 'sustained virological response' (SVR = undetectable HCV RNA) in over 95% of patients — regardless of genotype — with just 8-12 weeks of one or two tablets per day. Side effects are minimal (headache, fatigue in some). In India, generic versions of these medicines are manufactured by Indian pharmaceutical companies (Natco, Cipla, Sun Pharma) at dramatically reduced cost — a complete 12-week course of sofosbuvir + daclatasvir costs approximately Rs 5,000-10,000 from chemists or online pharmacies. The National Viral Hepatitis Control Programme (NVHCP) of the Government of India provides FREE HCV testing and treatment at government facilities — contact the nearest district hospital or government medical college hepatology department.

frequently_asked_questions.question: I tested positive for HBsAg — does this mean I have hepatitis B for life?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: A positive HBsAg means the hepatitis B surface antigen is present in your blood, indicating you currently have HBV. Whether this becomes permanent depends on when you were infected: adults who acquire HBV clear it spontaneously in 90-95% of cases within 6 months — only 5-10% become chronic carriers (HBsAg positive >6 months). However, babies infected at birth or young children infected in early life have a 90% chance of becoming chronic carriers. The key first steps after a positive HBsAg are: consult a hepatologist; get a full HBV panel (HBeAg, anti-HBe, HBV DNA viral load, LFTs, FibroScan); get vaccinated household and sexual contacts; complete alcohol abstinence; and get HCC surveillance (liver ultrasound + AFP every 6 months) if cirrhosis is present or risk is high. Antiviral therapy (tenofovir or entecavir) can suppress the virus and prevent disease progression — though it does not cure HBV. New 'cure' therapies are in clinical trials.

frequently_asked_questions.question: How do I know if someone has given me hepatitis? What should I do after a possible exposure?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: After possible exposure to HBV (needlestick, unprotected sex, blood splash): (1) Go immediately to a hospital emergency department — within 24-48 hours; Post-Exposure Prophylaxis (PEP) for HBV: Hepatitis B Immunoglobulin (HBIG) + HBV vaccine must be given within 24-48 hours of exposure for maximum protection; the sooner, the better. (2) Get tested for HBsAg and anti-HBs to determine your current status. After possible HCV exposure (needlestick with HCV-positive blood, IV needle sharing): no PEP vaccine or immunoglobulin exists for HCV; get an HCV RNA test at 4-6 weeks and anti-HCV at 3-6 months after exposure; if HCV RNA positive on early testing — contact a hepatologist immediately as treating acute HCV (before it becomes chronic) with 8 weeks of DAAs achieves near-100% cure rates. For HAV: post-exposure prophylaxis with HAV vaccine or IVIG within 2 weeks of exposure provides protection.

frequently_asked_questions.question: Is it safe to breastfeed my baby if I have hepatitis B?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: Yes — breastfeeding is SAFE for HBsAg-positive mothers, provided the baby has received the standard PMTCT protocol at birth: Hepatitis B Immunoglobulin (HBIG) injection within 12 hours of birth PLUS the first dose of HBV vaccine within 12-24 hours of birth. Multiple large studies have confirmed that breastfeeding does not increase HBV transmission risk when the infant has received HBIG and the birth-dose vaccine. The benefits of breastfeeding (nutrition, immunity, bonding) significantly outweigh any theoretical risk. Complete the 3-dose HBV vaccine series and test the infant at 9-12 months to confirm successful protection. The only exception is if nipples are severely cracked and bleeding — temporarily pause breastfeeding until healed.

frequently_asked_questions.question: Can I drink alcohol if I have hepatitis B or C?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: No — there is no safe level of alcohol consumption for patients with chronic hepatitis B or C. Alcohol and viral hepatitis act synergistically to damage the liver — the combination is far more harmful than either alone. Alcohol dramatically accelerates liver fibrosis and cirrhosis in patients with viral hepatitis (3-5 times faster progression in heavy drinkers). Alcohol also: impairs the immune response to HBV and HCV; increases HCC risk; worsens response to treatment; and in cirrhosis — ANY alcohol can trigger life-threatening complications (variceal bleeding, encephalopathy, decompensation). Post-SVR for HCV (after being cured) — alcohol remains harmful because any degree of liver damage or fibrosis persists and the liver's regenerative capacity has been impaired. The medical advice for all patients with viral hepatitis and chronic liver disease is: COMPLETE, PERMANENT ALCOHOL ABSTINENCE.

frequently_asked_questions.question: My doctor wants me to have a FibroScan — what is it and why is it important?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: A FibroScan (transient elastography) is a completely non-invasive, painless 5-minute scan of your liver done in the outpatient clinic. A small probe is placed on the skin over your liver and sends a mild vibration — the machine measures how stiff your liver is in kilopascals (kPa). The stiffer the liver, the more scar tissue (fibrosis) is present. This is critically important because: (1) It determines how urgently you need antiviral treatment — more fibrosis = more urgent; (2) It identifies whether you have cirrhosis — which changes your management completely (HCC surveillance, varices screening, transplant assessment); (3) It monitors whether fibrosis improves after treatment — liver stiffness can decrease after successful HCV cure (SVR) or with HBV suppression; (4) It avoids the need for a liver biopsy (which is invasive and has a small risk of bleeding) in most cases. Values >11-13 kPa suggest cirrhosis — this is an important threshold that triggers additional investigations and HCC surveillance.

frequently_asked_questions.question: What is the National Viral Hepatitis Control Programme (NVHCP) in India and how can I access free treatment?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: The National Viral Hepatitis Control Programme (NVHCP) was launched by the Government of India in 2018 as part of a national elimination strategy — with the goal of eliminating hepatitis B and C as public health threats by 2030. Key features: (1) FREE hepatitis B and C testing at government facilities; (2) FREE generic DAA treatment for hepatitis C (sofosbuvir-based regimens) at government medical colleges and district hospitals; (3) FREE HBV antiviral therapy (tenofovir) in selected facilities; (4) FREE HAV and HBV vaccination for high-risk groups; (5) Integration with PMTCT for pregnant women. To access: contact the nearest government medical college/AIIMS/PGIMER/other apex centre; district hospitals have treatment facilities; register under the Pradhan Mantri Jan Arogya Yojana (PMJAY / Ayushman Bharat) for further access. Call the national health helpline 1800-180-1104 for guidance. Private sector: generic DAA medicines from licensed pharmacies at low cost (Rs 5,000-15,000 for full course); ensure medicines are from approved WHO-prequalified manufacturers.
